binds.rule: F1 — Analytical usage reads only DAR.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: The marimo page may not issue a single query against das__raw, das__staged, dab, dab__stage or dab__meta, nor read the parquet lake directly — not even 'to check'. Its only legal source is dar__uss. It also forbids the page computing the count itself from an order-grain view: the measure must come from the bridge.

binds.rule: F2 — DAR reads only DAB.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: The USS generator and every statement in dar/sql may reference only dab.* objects. It forbids sourcing ship_country from das__staged.orders because the DAB view is awkward, and forbids building the calendar spine from das__staged order dates. The calendar's date range must derive from the DAB-sourced event dates.

binds.rule: F3 — DAB reads only DAS.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: The daana mapping's `table:` must name a das__staged object. It forbids pointing a mapping at the OData endpoint, at a parquet path, or at das__raw. Spike 2 F2 confirms this costs nothing: das__staged VIEWs over das__raw base tables were consumed 'with no complaint and no special configuration'.

binds.rule: Each movement between layers does exactly one job: ingest, integrate, specialise.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids the dlt resource deriving order_month; forbids das__staged resolving a business key; forbids the daana mapping computing the count; forbids the USS generator applying a business filter such as 'exclude cancelled'. Each of the four steps in slice 1 does one thing only.

binds.rule: S1 — Capture and persist only. No business logic, no interpretation, no enrichment.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: das__staged.orders may not carry order_month, a shipped/unshipped flag, a coalesced country, or a row filter. The order-month grain is a requirement and belongs in the USS event/calendar, not in DAS.

binds.rule: S2 — Non-volatile. Nothing updated, nothing deleted, every load retained.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids dlt write_disposition replace or merge; forbids a build step that clears das/… before reloading; forbids das__staged being a materialised table that is truncated. Spike 1 F12 confirms append is sufficient: two runs left both parquet files and both _dlt_loads rows intact.

binds.rule: S3 — Forgiving ingestion, strict unpacking.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids any type or schema commitment at ingest (spike 1 F5 shows max_table_nesting=0 is not enough — top-level keys still become typed columns), and equally forbids das__staged being a permissive passthrough. Every column in das__staged must be named by the contract; a field the contract does not name must land in the payload but must not appear downstream.

binds.rule: S4 — Every data point records where it came from and when.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids a landed row with no provenance and forbids relying on _dlt_id as identity — spike 1 F11 observed the same source record (OrderId 10248) getting a different _dlt_id in each load. It also forbids the load-completion timestamp being reachable only via the _dlt_loads JSONL side files (spike 1 F10); extracted_at must be on the row.

binds.rule: S5 — The source keeps its own words.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: das__staged columns must be order_id, order_date, ship_country, freight, ship_via — the mechanical snake_case of Northwind's own words. Forbids placed_on, country, order_placed_date. `ShipVia` and its ilk are explicitly not violations here.

binds.rule: B1/B2 — Subject oriented and source-agnostic.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids an entity named NORTHWIND_ORDER or ODATA_ORDER, and forbids the ORDER entity being a mirror of the OData Order type. Slice 1 declares only the attributes the question needs plus identity — not all fourteen Northwind properties because they happen to be in the payload.

binds.rule: B3/B4 — Time-variant and non-volatile: every version retained, none overwritten.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Constrains the mapping concretely: `entity_effective_timestamp_expression` must be extracted_at (spike 2 F6 observed this historises exactly as needed), and the ingestion strategy must not be one that overwrites. Combined with the observed FULL defect it effectively forces FULL_LOG (see tensions).

binds.rule: B5 — Atomic. No aggregation, no bucketing, no pre-rollup.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: dab/model.yaml may not declare ORDER_MONTH, ORDER_COUNT or a bucketed date. The entity carries the order's own date attribute; the month is produced by the calendar in DAR and the count by the bridge.

binds.rule: B6 — Reusable. Nothing exists here because one consumer wanted it.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids inventing a SHIP_COUNTRY entity solely so the page has a peripheral to group by. Ship country is an atomic property of the order and is modelled as an attribute; the peripheral is `order`.

binds.rule: B7 — Change is additive: a new attribute, entity or relationship is a new structure, never a modification.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Binds slice 1's shape rather than its content: the entity must be laid out so slice 2 adds rather than edits. It forbids modelling the order as one wide structure whose next attribute is an ALTER — which daana's _desc model already prevents, and which slice 1 must not work around.

binds.rule: B8 — Meaning is defined exactly once, here.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: The DAS contract's `description` may not say what an order means to the business; the marimo page may not restate a definition; the question file may not define 'order placed' differently from dab/model.yaml. Every definition string lives in model.yaml and everything else references it.

binds.rule: R4 — Volatile and generated. Nothing here is hand-written or hand-edited.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids hand-writing dar/sql/*.sql, hand-fixing a column name in the generated bridge, and hand-writing the calendar. A wrong name in dar__uss is fixed in dab/model.yaml or dab/uss.yaml and regenerated.

binds.rule: R5 — What was delivered, to whom, and when is recorded.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids treating 'the page renders' as the whole of acceptance. Nothing in the repo currently records a delivery; slice 1 either implements something (an export or screenshot tied to a commit) or acknowledges the gap in the ADR rather than passing over it silently.

binds.rule: The layers are called das, dab and dar literally, in schemas, directories and prose.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids the schemas landing as das_raw, raw, staging or main. Spike 1 F13 observed dlt silently collapsing das__raw to das_raw with only a WARNING; enable_dataset_name_normalization=False is mandatory, not optional.

binds.rule: A contract file's stem is the landed table name, used in every schema of this layer.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: das/contracts/orders.yaml → das__raw.orders → das__staged.orders → the mapping's `table: das__staged.orders`. Forbids a contract named northwind_orders.yaml landing a table called orders, or vice versa.

binds.rule: Columns this layer adds itself carry no source's word and are named for what they record: extracted_at, extracted_on, payload.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Fixes the staged view's own columns to exactly those names. It bears directly on whether _dlt_load_id may cross into das__staged at all (see tensions).

binds.rule: DAB entity, attribute and relationship identifiers are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, singular, with id and name holding the identical string; no source name appears anywhere in DAB.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: ORDER, ORDER_ID, SHIP_COUNTRY, PLACED_ON — not Order, not order_id, not ORDERS. Forbids a definition mentioning Northwind, OData, or the Orders feed. Spike 2 F3 shows DuckDB carries that casing into object names, which is the first tension below.

binds.rule: DAR object names are snake_case singular; a reserved word is quoted, never abbreviated around; key column is <object>_key; attribute columns are the lower-cased attribute identifier unchanged; structural columns carry a leading underscore; measure columns are _measure__<entity>__<measure>.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: The peripheral is dar__uss."order" — not ord, not orders, not order_dim. The key is order_key. The attribute column is ship_country. The bridge carries _bridge, _stage, _event, _event_date and _calendar. Spike 4 F4 confirms sqlfluff's duckdb dialect accepts dab."order" without complaint.

binds.rule: Measure names are <descriptor>_<entities>_<unit>: entity part plural, no scope or aggregation words, a real unit, no stored ratios.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: The one measure is placed_orders_count — the document's own worked example. Forbids order_count, total_orders, count_of_orders, num_orders, orders_by_month.

binds.rule: SQL style: duckdb dialect, keywords upper, functions lower, four-space indent, one expression per line, every expression aliased with AS, every table reference aliased, every column table-qualified in a multi-table statement, cast() never ::, DAB identifiers double-quoted, no SELECT * in anything a consumer reads, and SQL living in a Python string is written to a file so the same linter sees it.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Binds the generator's emit and binds the marimo page: the page's query may not be an inline Python string — it must be a .sql file the sqlfluff hook lints. Spike 4 F5 shows RF02 is the one rule sqlfluff cannot autofix, so the generator must table-qualify from the start.

binds.rule: YAML: two-space indent, lines ≤160, flow mappings only for short homogeneous rows and never column-aligned, booleans true/false.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Binds das/contracts/orders.yaml, dab/model.yaml, dab/uss.yaml and dab/mappings/*.yaml. `effective_timestamp: true`, never yes. Contract column rows may be flow mappings but must not be padded into columns.

binds.rule: No data vocabulary anywhere under src/ or in test code — no entity, attribute or business term from the model appears in the machinery or in a test. Test fixtures use neutral models held as data files.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids the strings order, ship_country, northwind or placed_orders_count appearing in src/adss/**; forbids a test named test_orders_per_month; forbids the acceptance queries being literals in tests/. The queries must be data files the runner discovers.

binds.rule: Machinery is test-first; data checks assert the built warehouse and land with the build that satisfies them; no pytest.skip and no imperative xfail; a failing check is fixed by fixing the code or making the configuration honest, never by weakening the test.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids the two-query agreement check being skipped when no warehouse exists, and forbids marking it xfail until the build works. It forces the question of when the warehouse is built relative to the gate (see tensions).

binds.rule: Conventional commits with layer scopes; one question per slice; branch claude/adss-slice-NN-<slug> off the previous slice; stacked branches rebased not merged; every commit passes the gate and the whole suite on its own; an ADR lands before the code it decides.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids code in this slice before its ADRs exist — including the DAR ADR that D-0001 already cites and which is currently missing. Forbids a single omnibus commit: das, dab, dar, questions and destination each carry their own scope, and each intermediate commit must be green.

binds.rule: A decision goes in a numbered MADR under docs/adr/ and is superseded by a new file rather than edited; a departure from a blueprint principle or a hard rule needs an entry in deviations.md and an ADR.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids editing 0000; forbids a deviation registered without an argument behind it; requires docs/adr/README.md's index to list every new record. ADR 0000's own Confirmation makes this a review check, not an automated one.

binds.rule: When a rule does not fit there are exactly three recourses — clarify the page, register a deviation, or change the rule. A quiet exception is not on the list.
binds.whatItForbidsHere: Forbids resolving any tension below by reading a word narrowly and moving on. Every item in the next section must end in a written change to conventions.md, an entry in deviations.md with an ADR, or a superseded ADR.

tensions.rule: blueprint.md F1 — 'Analytical usage reads only DAR.'
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: The already-decided acceptance mechanism computes every question twice, once from das__staged and once from dar__uss. Computing a business answer from das__staged is, read plainly, the thing F1 forbids. Worse than the flow breach is the definitional one: the control query is a second expression of 'orders placed per order month and ship country', written in DAS source vocabulary, living outside dab/model.yaml — exactly what B8 exists to prevent ('Definitions that exist in two places drift'). The control query's purpose is to surface drift, but nothing in the repo says which side is authoritative when they disagree, and §6 forbids fixing a failing check by weakening it. There is also a shelf life: the das__staged expression stays writable only while a question needs no integration. From the first question that spans two sources, writing it against das__staged means reimplementing DAB inside the check.
tensions.resolution: Register a deviation. This is F1 exactly, done knowingly, for a good reason — not a case the rule was never aimed at. The tempting alternative is to clarify that a CI check is not 'analytical usage'; it is defensible (F1 says analytical usage, and a regression check is engineering usage) and it is what most teams would do, but it works by narrowing a word in an absolute rule to make the thing you want fall outside it, and the next person uses the same move for a notebook that 'is just a check'. The register's own words settle it: an unregistered exception is indistinguishable from a mistake. Recommended entry — Cost: every question carries a second definition in source vocabulary that must be maintained in lockstep, and a disagreement has no declared arbiter. Exit condition: the first question whose das__staged expression cannot be written without reimplementing DAB integration; at that point the control query is deleted and replaced by machinery tests of the generator.

tensions.rule: conventions.md §1.2 — DAB identifiers are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, with id and name holding the identical string.
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: Spike 2 F3 observed that DuckDB is case-preserving, so model.yaml casing lands verbatim in object names: 'Entity id CUSTOMER produced view_CUSTOMER, CUSTOMER_focal, ORDER_CUSTOMER_x — not the lowercase view_customer the PostgreSQL run produced.' Slice 1 therefore gets dab.view_ORDER, dab.ORDER_desc, ORDER_key, and — since the spike's working model used lowercase attribute ids and produced lowercase columns — UPPER attribute ids will produce columns ORDER_ID, SHIP_COUNTRY, PLACED_ON. Every DAR statement must then double-quote them (§3), RF06 must stay excluded (it already is, and spike 4 confirms six hits in a six-column view), and spike 2's gotcha warns that 'code that string-matches names out of information_schema WILL break' — which the USS generator must do, and which is further complicated by spike 2 F13: the views are wrappers over table macros that do not appear in information_schema at all. Separately, the rule's stated reason — 'It is the modelling language's convention' — is no longer true of the tool: the blog records that daana-cli 0.7.0 accepts any casing and removed the entity-name-casing, attribute-type-casing and relationship-name-casing lint rules.
tensions.resolution: Clarify the rule. Keep UPPER_SNAKE_CASE — its real value is the second reason given, that the visual break makes a leak obvious on sight, and that reason survives the tool's change. Add three sentences: the rule governs identifiers in dab/model.yaml and dab/uss.yaml only; the generator lower-cases on the way into DAR (§1.3 already says this for attribute columns, not for object or key names — say it for those too); and any read of the catalog is case-normalised and must also query duckdb_functions(), because the macros the views depend on are invisible to information_schema. The honest alternative is to change the rule to lowercase ids: it would delete an entire class of quoting bugs, remove the need to exclude RF06, and cost nothing with the tool as it now stands. Reject it, but on the record — it also deletes the property that makes a business term leaking into another layer visible at a glance, and makes the DAB identifier and the DAR object name textually identical.

tensions.rule: blueprint.md S1 — 'Capture and persist only. No business logic, no interpretation, no enrichment.'
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: das__staged unpacks the payload and casts: OrderDate to DATE, Freight to DECIMAL. A cast is a decision, and spike 1 F16 shows it is a consequential one — dlt infers freight as DOUBLE, the explicit cast makes it DECIMAL(18,4), and the finding calls that 'a concrete argument for the two-layer design'. It is also an interpretation of what the source meant by a number. The blueprint contains both S1 (no interpretation) and S3 (enforce structure at the boundary out), and the blog corpus records the same collision as unresolved: the synthesis lists it under contradictions — 'Either the blueprint's DAS is only the landing zone (and staging is unlabelled), or the staging step violates a stated absolute.' The sharpest instance in slice 1 is null handling: Northwind's $metadata declares OrderDate as a nullable Edm.Date, so a cast that silently yields NULL asserts 'this order has no date', and a cast that raises makes a schema commitment at the boundary out.
tensions.resolution: Clarify the rule — the blueprint is the fixed point and cannot be edited to fit. Add to conventions §1.1 the line the blueprint deliberately leaves out: structural conformance is not interpretation. A cast to the type the source's own metadata declares is transcription and is required; a cast that chooses between plausible types, a COALESCE, a default value, a rename, or a row filter is business logic and belongs in DAB. Northwind publishes $metadata (Edm.Int32, Edm.Date, Edm.String, Edm.Decimal), so slice 1's contract can be justified as transcription of a published declaration rather than a judgement — which is a strong position and worth writing down while it is true. If the team is unwilling to hold that line, the honest move is a deviation, not silence.

tensions.rule: blueprint.md R4 — 'Volatile and generated. Nothing here is hand-written or hand-edited', and conventions.md §1.3 'Nothing in this layer is hand-edited.'
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: The repo already carries an empty dar/sql/ directory and .gitignore excludes the warehouse but not generated SQL, so slice 1 will commit generator output. Committing is not editing, but it creates a second copy of the truth with nothing checking it: nothing in the repo asserts that dar/sql at HEAD equals what the generator emits from dab/model.yaml and dab/uss.yaml at HEAD. Spike 4 compounds it by recommending 'run sqlfluff fix as a generation post-step rather than teaching the generator about newlines' — if fix runs outside the generator, the committed artefact is not generator output and regeneration produces a spurious diff every time. Meanwhile §3's whole justification is that generated-SQL diffs are read constantly, which only pays off if the committed file is trustworthy.
tensions.resolution: Clarify the rule, and add the missing mechanism. Write into conventions §1.3 that generated artefacts are committed and that the gate regenerates and fails on any difference (a regenerate step followed by git diff --exit-code). That keeps R4 literally true — the file is never the source — preserves the diff-readability §3 is built around, and forces sqlfluff fix to live inside the generator rather than in someone's hands. The alternative, gitignoring dar/sql like the .duckdb file, is cleaner against R4 but throws away reviewable diffs of the one layer nobody writes by hand, and makes a generator regression invisible until someone runs it. Recommend committing plus the regeneration check; name its cost, which is a slower gate and a build step that must be deterministic down to whitespace.

tensions.rule: blueprint.md S4 — 'Every data point records where it came from and when.'
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: The landed row is payload plus dlt's two columns. Spike 1 F9 is explicit: 'dlt adds EXACTLY TWO metadata columns to a root table: _dlt_load_id and _dlt_id. Nothing else. They are NOT sufficient for which load, from where, when.' The decided design elects _dlt_load_id as the single provenance fact, which answers when (load time, not source event time) and which load, but not from where — no source system, no request URL, no entity — except by inference from the table name and the partition path, neither of which is a column. Spike 1 F18 shows the conforming option was available and declined: hand-added das_source_system, das_request_url, das_http_status, das_page_number all 'pass through untouched'. Second, S4 says data point, not row. One blob per record makes a field's provenance the record's provenance — which is true only while one contract reads one endpoint into one row, and stops being true the moment a landed row composes two responses.
tensions.resolution: Clarify the rule, with a condition attached. Write into conventions §1.1 that a landed record is by construction one whole source record from one response, so record-level provenance is per-data-point provenance; that composing a landed row from more than one response is forbidden, because it silently voids that equivalence; and that 'from where' is carried by the contract stem and the partition path, naming why no source-identity column exists (one source, one endpoint per contract). If the team is not willing to forbid composition outright, this is not a clarification but a deviation and must be registered as one. Do not leave it as it is: as written, the design satisfies S4 by an argument nobody has written down, which is the same as not satisfying it.

tensions.rule: conventions.md §5 — 'No data vocabulary anywhere under src/ or in test code.'
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: The slice's acceptance is that two business queries agree. Those queries are pure business vocabulary — ship_country, order_date, _measure__order__placed_orders_count. As literals in tests/ they break the rule outright, and moving them to src/ breaks the same rule. The rule already names its own escape ('Test fixtures use neutral models held as data files'), and README.md already promises docs/questions/ holding 'the business questions, and the two queries that must agree on each answer' — but conventions.md says nothing about what a question file is, where it lives, or that it is the vehicle that keeps the test generic. Slice 1 will invent that format silently, in the one place the whole slice is accepted.
tensions.resolution: Clarify the rule. State that a question is a data file under docs/questions/ carrying the question text, the two SQL bodies and the expected shape; that the runner in tests/ discovers question files and asserts agreement without naming anything; and that no test may contain an entity, attribute, measure or source name. Pin the file format in §4 while you are there. Two consequences worth writing down: the question SQL must be .sql files so the existing sqlfluff pre-commit hook (types: [sql]) lints them like everything else — §3's 'SQL that lives in a Python string is written to a file' already demands this — and the runner must be parameterised, because a hand-written per-question test function reintroduces the vocabulary through its own name.

tensions.rule: conventions.md §6 — data checks assert what the built warehouse contains, no pytest.skip and no imperative xfail; and §7 — every commit passes the gate and the whole suite on its own.
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: The gate is `uv run pre-commit run --all-files`, whose pytest hook runs the whole suite with pass_filenames: false. The warehouse is gitignored (*.duckdb) so it is never in a fresh checkout, and CI does nothing but sync and run the gate. From the first commit of slice 1 the data check therefore runs with no warehouse: it cannot skip (§6), it cannot pass, and 'every commit is green' collapses. Building the warehouse inside every gate run is not free either — spike 2 F11 found that any other open connection, 'read-write OR READ-ONLY', makes daana-cli execute fail with the misleading 'daana framework is not installed on the remote database', and spike 4 notes sqlfluff is already the slowest hook.
tensions.resolution: Clarify the rule and make the configuration honest — which §6 explicitly permits as the alternative to weakening a test. Split the suite: the local pre-commit pytest hook runs machinery tests only; CI builds the warehouse from das/fixtures before running the gate, then runs the data checks as an explicitly-invoked suite. That requires §7's 'the whole suite' to say which suite, and requires the build step to exist in ci.yml before slice 1's first data check lands. Reject the tempting shortcut of a fixture that fabricates a warehouse for the check: §6's second row forbids exactly that ('Data checks are not written against a stub'), and a check that passes against a stub tells you nothing about the build.

tensions.rule: conventions.md §8 — a departure from a principle needs an entry in deviations.md and an ADR; §7 — an ADR lands before the code it decides; deviations.md — 'Every deviation has one; the register is the index, the ADR is the argument.'
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: D-0001 cites adr/0002-dar-is-one-generated-unified-star-schema.md. That file does not exist. docs/adr/ contains only 0000-use-madr.md, and docs/adr/README.md's index lists only 0000. So the one open deviation in the register — the one slice 1's entire DAR design rests on — currently has no argument behind it and is not in the index. By the register's own review standard ('a defect in the same way a failing test is'), this is already broken, and slice 1 is the commit that would build on it.
tensions.resolution: Not one of the three recourses — it is a defect to fix, and it blocks. ADR 0002 must land before any dar-scoped code in this slice, together with whatever 0001 is meant to be, and docs/adr/README.md's index must list them. Recommend treating the missing ADR as a gate on the dar commit specifically, not on the slice as a whole, so das and dab work is not held hostage to it.

tensions.rule: conventions.md §1.2 — 'No source name appears anywhere in DAB — not in an id, not in a definition, not in a description.'
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: dab/mappings/orders-mapping.yaml must contain `table: das__staged.orders`, `primary_keys: [order_id]` and `transformation_expression: ship_country` — source words, in files under dab/. Spike 2 F2 shows exactly that shape working. Read literally, §1.2 is violated by every mapping file the system will ever contain, and the first reviewer applying it as a hard rule blocks the first mapping in the slice. The same problem reaches dab/uss.yaml, which sits in dab/ but declares DAR things and must follow §1.3 and §2 rather than §1.2.
tensions.resolution: Clarify the rule. The rule is aimed at the vocabulary DAB publishes; the mapping is the one artefact whose entire job is to bind two vocabularies and it cannot do that without naming both. Write the line explicitly: source names may appear in dab/mappings/** in `table`, `primary_keys` and `transformation_expression` and nowhere else; dab/model.yaml carries no source name in an id, name, definition or description; dab/uss.yaml is governed by §1.3 and §2, not §1.2, because it is a DAR declaration that happens to live beside the model. Without those three sentences the directory has two naming regimes and nothing says which key falls under which.

tensions.rule: conventions.md §1.3 'Measure columns are _measure__<entity>__<measure>' against §2 'Pattern: <descriptor>_<entities>_<unit>', entity part plural.
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: Slice 1's single measure resolves to _measure__order__placed_orders_count — the entity appears twice, singular from §1.3 and plural inside the measure name from §2. The blog's own worked example is _measure__order_line__revenue: a bare measure word in the third segment, not the three-part name. So the convention document and the source it derives from disagree about what the third segment holds, and slice 1 must encode one of them in the generator, permanently, on its first run.
tensions.resolution: Clarify the rule — say which, in §1.3, with an example. Recommend keeping the full §2 name in the third segment (_measure__order__placed_orders_count): §2 is a hard rule whose stated payoff is searchability 'by any of the three' parts, and that only holds if the whole name survives into the physical column. Name the cost honestly: the columns get long and repetitive, and §1.3's claim that two underscores make the three segments unambiguous gets harder to read once the third segment contains single underscores of its own.

tensions.rule: blueprint.md B3 — 'Time-variant. Historized: every version retained, none overwritten', with its reason 'An answer served last quarter must still be reproducible this quarter, or the system cannot be audited.'
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: Spike 2 F9 observed that ingestion_strategy: FULL against a source view holding more than one row per primary key inserts 'exactly ONE duplicate _desc row per execute — same key, same type_key, same seq_nbr, same eff_tmstp, same value', growing 22 → 23 → 24 → 25 across three runs, and that 'NONE of the presentation views show it: view_CUSTOMER stayed at 3 rows and view_CUSTOMER_hist at 4 rows the whole time'. The decided DAS design — append-only parquet, one row per key per load — makes das__staged.orders multi-row-per-key by construction, which is precisely the triggering input. Nothing in conventions.md constrains the strategy, so slice 1 picks one silently. The compounding problem is that the slice's headline safety net is blind to it: both the das__staged control query and the dar__uss query read through views that mask the duplication, so the two queries agree while the history quietly corrupts.
tensions.resolution: Clarify the rule — add a hard rule to conventions §1.2 or a new mapping section: mappings use FULL_LOG; FULL is permitted only against a source view proven to hold exactly one row per key, and the proof is a data check, not a claim. Pair it with a data check that counts dab.<ENTITY>_desc rows across two consecutive executes and fails on growth, because that base table is the only place the defect is visible. Also record in the DAB ADR that this is an unadvertised-platform risk: spike 2 notes daana-cli's own help text lists PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, Oracle and SQL Server and does not mention DuckDB, so 'do not expect DuckDB parity to be maintained by the vendor'.

tensions.rule: The decided constraint 'One DuckDB file, platform behind one seam', together with conventions.md §7 'every commit passes the gate'.
tensions.howSliceOneStrainsIt: Spike 2 F11 found that any other open connection to the file — including a read-only one — makes daana-cli execute fail, and that the error it reports is a lie: 'daana framework is not installed on the remote database. Run daana-cli install first', with no lock, conflict or duckdb string anywhere even at debug level. Slice 1 puts three processes on one file: dlt writing, daana-cli writing, marimo reading. Spike 3's gotcha is the mirror image — 'a marimo app holding a read-write handle will block dlt or daana-cli'. Nothing in the repo states a writer discipline, so the first CI failure will be misdiagnosed as a broken install.
tensions.resolution: Clarify the rule — this is a design constraint the documents simply do not carry. result.argument:
**Why a machinery model is not a restatement, and what would make it one.**

The two models are disjoint universes of discourse with orthogonal rates of change, and that orthogonality is measurable rather than rhetorical. `dab/model.yaml` answers "what is an ORDER, and how does it relate to a CUSTOMER". `src/adss/` answers "which relation does this step read, where does a landed file go, what does a contract column cast to". Swap the business — replace Northwind with a payroll source — and `dab/`, `das/contracts/`, `docs/questions/` are rewritten while `src/` changes by not one character. Swap the platform — DuckDB for Postgres, daana-cli for something else — and `src/` changes substantially while `dab/model.yaml` does not change at all. Two models whose populations move on different axes are not two copies of one model. The machinery model's population is *closed by the already-decided architecture*: six schemas, one landing layout, one provenance rule, five movements. The business model's population grows with every slice. That is the test, and it gives the decision a falsifiable tripwire: **if adding a business entity requires a change under `src/`, the machinery model has become a restatement.** Slice 2 is the first real trial of it.

It becomes a restatement by six identifiable moves, and each should block a review: a type or union variant named after a business concept (`OrderStep`); a field whose *name* comes from the model (`Contract.order_id`); a default or branch keyed on a business value (`if entity_id == "ORDER"`); interpreting the `definition:` string for anything but pass-through — the moment code reads a definition to *decide* something, meaning has a second home and conventions §1.2's "that is the **only** place the data is explained" is false; widening `EntityRef` with semantics DAB already carries (`grain`, `subject_area`, `is_dimension`); and any codegen that writes Python into `src/` from the model. The parsing itself is not a restatement, and the line is precise: the machinery may know that a model *has* entities; it may not know that ORDER is one. It carries the definition string through untouched and never reads it.

**What "no business vocabulary under src/" buys, and what actually enforces it.**

Four things, none of them aesthetic. First, genericity by construction rather than by claim — a machinery that cannot name a source cannot special-case one, which is the only mechanism by which "a change costs about the same in year ten as in year one" can be true. Second, it forces every business decision into the declarative artefacts, which is where the blog's "the definition *is* the implementation" requires them and where the double-definition failure (B8) is prevented. Third — and this is the argument I would lead with — **the blueprint's absolutes only become executable if the machinery has types for the seams.** F1 ("analytical usage reads only DAR") is prose until `Destination.reads: frozenset[Relation]` exists and a test asserts every element's `.schema.layer is Layer.DAR`. F3 is prose until a mapping's source relation is typed and checked to live in `das__staged`. A blueprint that "contains no exceptions and no pre-authorised bypass" but no check is a blueprint enforced by memory, and the corpus is explicit that "a rule the agent has to remember is weaker than a rule the platform enforces" (context-isnt-enough). Fourth, agent legibility: a per-entity branch in code is exactly the per-entity special case that erodes "an agent that learns the shape of one entity knows the shape of all of them".

Is the hard rule enough on its own? No — and the conventions document's own logic leaves a hole here. It says "where an off-the-shelf tool can already check a rule, the tool's configuration is the rule … everything else is checked by whoever — or whatever — reviews the change." No off-the-shelf tool checks this rule, so by that logic it falls entirely to review, which is precisely where the blog says conventions die: "People agree in the moment, then forget when they're actually writing code." But the conventions' anti-drift principle rightly forbids the usual remedy, a hand-written denylist, because that is a second machine-readable copy of the model. There is a third path the document does not rule out and which cannot drift: **derive the denylist from the artefacts at check time.** The identifiers in `dab/model.yaml` and the table stems, `source_path`s and `target_name`s in `das/contracts/*.yaml` already *are* a machine-readable list of exactly the words that must not appear in `src/`. Nothing is kept in sync, because the rule is the model. Add an entity and the check widens by itself. The context-blindness the blog objects to — "Is `total_orders` wrong because it uses a forbidden word, or is it acceptable because it's a column in a source table you don't control?" — does not arise, because §1.1's source-vocabulary exemption applies to DAS *object and column names*, i.e. YAML and SQL, and the check scans only `src/` and `tests/`, where no exemption exists.

That gives three tiers, in descending strength and matching the corpus's own two-tier alignment. Behavioural: the machinery suite runs against neutral fixture systems and never against `dab/` or `das/contracts/` — this *proves* genericity rather than asserting it, exactly as conventions §5 demands. Lexical: the derived denylist, which catches the residual case behaviour cannot, a business word used in a *name* rather than in behaviour. Judgement: review against conventions.md, human or agent, which is the only tier that catches a synonym (`purchase` for ORDER) or a Northwind-shaped constant with no Northwind word in it (`if len(columns) == 14`). I am recommending all three, and I am saying plainly that the first is the one that matters.

**Neutral fixtures, and why they are a capability rather than a tax.**

A neutral fixture is a whole miniature system held in files: a contract, a recorded source payload, a model, a USS sidecar, a mapping, a question and its two SQL files, and an `expected/` directory of emitted artefacts. The test bodies name nothing: they are parameterised over the fixture directory and derive expectations from the fixture's own declarations, so the same test body passes over structurally different fixtures. Two fixtures, not one, is what makes the claim testable — with one fixture a hardcoded shape assumption passes green.

The vocabulary criteria are three: absent from the real model *and* from any source the system could plausibly ingest; concrete enough that a failing assertion still tells you which thing broke; and obviously fictional so nobody mistakes it for a slice. `foo/bar/baz` fails the second. `INVOICE`/`PAYMENT` fails the first and third — neutral today, a business term in slice 7. A deliberately non-commercial concrete domain passes all three; `PEBBLE` with `PEBBLE_COLOUR` and `FOUND_ON`, event `FOUND`, measure `found_pebbles_count`, is the shape I would use, and the name matters less than the criteria.

The reframe that matters: **the neutral fixture stages failure modes the real source cannot.** Spike 1 observed that "a plain read_parquet glob over an append-only lake SILENTLY DROPS columns added in later loads — no error, just missing data." To pin that against Northwind you would have to fabricate a schema change in the recording — i.e. fabricate data anyway. A fixture with a second load carrying a new column, a reserved-word entity id, a mixed-case source property and a nullable column tests evolution, quoting and lateness on day one. The fixture is not a purity device; it is the only place the awkward cases live.

**The typed shape, and the honest cost.**

Spike 4 removes the usual objection to this style: `ty --error all` over a module of frozen slotted dataclasses, `StrEnum`, `tuple[Column, ...]`, a `A | B | C` union alias and `match`/`assert_never` returned "All checks passed!" — zero false positives — while catching a frozen-field assignment, a wrong-union argument and an out-of-`Literal` discriminator. So the types cost nothing in gate friction and pay in the three shapes the spikes proved catchable. `frozen` is not decoration here: a mutable `Contract` lets a later step rewrite the contract mid-build, which is R4's hand-edit failure expressed in Python. `tuple` over `list` because a frozen dataclass with a list field is only shallowly immutable. `StrEnum` for `Schema`/`ColumnType` because members are usable directly in emitted SQL without `.value`; `Literal` for the step discriminator, because that is the shape spike 4 proved ty narrows.

But the abstraction cost is real and the corpus names it precisely: "Instead of undocumented transformations, you risk overly generic models lacking domain specificity", and "premature abstraction before patterns emerge adds overhead without benefit. Build a few implementations, discover commonalities, then abstract." Slice 1 has exactly one of everything — one contract, one entity, one event, one measure, one question, one destination — so every abstraction here is unfalsified by induction. My answer is narrow and I want it read as narrow: these types describe artefacts *already fixed by decisions taken*, not patterns guessed at. The six schemas, the hive layout, the `_dlt_load_id` provenance rule, the sidecar `uss.yaml`, the one CLI — none of them is inferred. Where the type would be inferred, I am cutting it. So: **no `MeasureKind`** — a one-member enum is the textbook case, and a count in an event-grain bridge needs no aggregation declaration at all. **No `Relationship`, no `Cardinality`, no walk** — the USS traversal rule ("follow any path that never fans out, and inherit everything along it") is real machinery, and with one entity it is a no-op; building it now is modelling slice 2. **No `Materialisation`** — everything slice 1 emits is a view. **No structured `Question`** — decomposing into aggregation/measure/dimension would re-declare what `uss.yaml` owns, which is a B8 violation wearing a type annotation.

The one type I want to argue *against* as well as for is `Plan`/`Step`. Five steps in fixed order is a list of five function calls, and a discriminated union over them is dead weight — unless the flow test is written against it. It earns its place only because F1–F3 become a property you can assert on the plan without executing it, and because `assert_never` fails the gate in slice 2 until every match handles the new kind. If that test is dropped, the abstraction is exactly the overhead the blog warns about and should be deleted. I would rather state that condition than pretend the union is self-justifying.

One naming hazard to fix now: **`stage` is overloaded three ways** — `das__staged`, `dab__stage`, and the USS `_stage` structural column, which is Puppini's per-entity role marker. The machinery's plan unit must therefore not be called `Stage`. Call it `Step`, and reserve `Stage` for the DAR concept. The cost is that code and artefacts then use different words for adjacent things; the alternative is a word with three referents in one repository.

**The alternatives, argued.**

*Plain dicts or TypedDicts* is the honest cheap option and the corpus points at it: "For three source tables, just hand-write the SQL and move on with your life. The overhead of maintaining contracts and a generator isn't justified when you can see the entire staging layer on a single screen." Slice 1 is one source table. Its real strength is that the YAML already is the model and Python that merely walks it is not pretending otherwise. Rejecting it costs a vocabulary a reader must learn before reading a five-line function. It fails on two counts. Spike 4 observed that ty over an untyped `dict` yields `missing-type-argument` and `unsound-return-statement` with the value "Inferred as `Unknown`" — so `ty --error all`, which conventions §5 makes the hard type gate, would be checking essentially nothing on the layer where the decisions live, and `d["colummns"]` fails at run time. TypedDict answers that objection and is a genuinely close call; it loses on a narrower point — no methods means no single home for the derived rules, so `union_by_name`, `extracted_on = date(_dlt_load_id)` and the DAB quoting rule scatter to call sites. All three of those are places the spikes found *silent* failure, which is the worst kind to scatter.

*A typed model mirrored from `dab/model.yaml`* — generate Python types per entity — is what many good systems do, and it buys something this decision gives up: a wrong attribute id becomes a check-time error rather than a run-time disagreement between the two computations. That is a real loss and I am naming it. It is rejected because it violates conventions §5 outright and would need a registered deviation; because a generated copy of the model in `src/` is the second documentation surface the corpus forbids ("These aren't three separate artifacts that can drift - they're the same source"); because R4's no-hand-editing rule would then apply to source code, with the diff noise of a regenerated `src/` on every slice; and because it is precisely the restatement the user ruled out.

*Pydantic* deserves more respect than a one-liner. The YAML is untrusted input; pydantic gives per-field errors with paths for free, which frozen dataclasses do not. Rejecting it means hand-writing parse errors. I reject it for slice 1 on three grounds, one of which is weak and I will say so: it puts a runtime dependency into the type signatures the whole system passes around; validation belongs at the parse seam where the error can name the file and the key, not in the domain types; and ty's behaviour with pydantic is simply *not observed* — spike 4 tested stdlib dataclasses only, and noted ty is "0.0.78 — pre-1.0 … expect diagnostic names/severities to churn." That third ground is an absence of evidence, not evidence. Pydantic remains the right answer for the parse module specifically if hand-written errors get bad, and nothing here forecloses it.

*SQL, templates and shell, with no Python domain* is the fewest-parts option: dlt lands, daana-cli integrates, staged views and the USS are SQL. Rejecting it costs building and maintaining a CLI and a plan for five steps. It fails because the decisions that are *not* SQL — which contract, which glob, which relation, in which order, with the warehouse connection closed before daana-cli runs — end up in a Makefile where nothing is typed and F1–F3 cannot be asserted; because `uv run adss ...` is already decided; and because the double-computation harness needs pytest regardless. Spike 2's observation that a held connection makes `execute` fail with the wholly misleading "daana framework is not installed on the remote database" is the kind of lifecycle rule that needs an owner, and a shell script is a poor one.

**One consequence that requires action outside this ADR.** The slice-1 destination is a marimo page under `destinations/`, it is Python, and both the ruff and ty hooks match `types_or: [python, pyi]`. It *must* name the business — axis labels, `_measure__…` columns. Conventions §5 scopes the rule to "under `src/` or in test code", so the page is already outside it, but §5's companion row lists the artefact homes as "the YAML, SQL and Markdown artefacts" and does not name a Python page. Per §9.1 the cheapest recourse is to clarify conventions.md — one line naming `destinations/` as an artefact directory — not to register a deviation. Generating the page from the question and the USS declarations would remove the ambiguity, but the page is the prototype the slice is accepted on, and generating it in slice 1 is premature.

result.confirmation:
**Primary — `tests/test_vocabulary.py::test_no_declared_name_appears_in_machinery`.** Collect every identifier declared in the real artefacts: entity, attribute and relationship ids from `dab/model.yaml`; table stems, `source_path`s and column `name`s from `das/contracts/*.yaml`; measure and event ids from `dab/uss.yaml` — each in both its declared casing and lower case. Subtract `tests/vocabulary_collisions.txt`. Assert none appears as a whole word token in any file under `src/` or `tests/`, excluding `tests/fixtures/`. The denylist is derived at check time from the artefacts themselves, so there is no second copy to drift. This test fails the day someone types `order` in a module or a test name.

**Negative control — `tests/test_vocabulary.py::test_the_check_fails_on_a_planted_word`.** Point the same collector at a synthetic tree under `tests/fixtures/vocabulary/` containing one planted violation and assert it is reported, with its file and line. A checker that has never been seen to fail is not a checker, and conventions §6 forbids expressing this as a skip or an `xfail`.

**Behavioural, and the stronger of the two — `tests/test_fixtures.py`, parameterised over `tests/fixtures/systems/*`.** The whole machinery suite builds each neutral fixture system end to end from its own directory, with `das/contracts/` and `dab/` of the real system never read. Expectations are derived from the fixture's declarations and diffed against the checked-in `expected/*.sql` and `expected/answer.csv`. The same test bodies pass over both `basic/` and `awkward/`. This is the test that *proves* genericity rather than asserting it, per conventions §5; running the suite with the real `dab/` and `das/contracts/` moved aside must still be green.

**Flow rules — `tests/test_flow.py::test_plan_respects_the_direction_of_flow`.** Over the plan built for each fixture: every `Step`'s `reads` are in a layer strictly below its `writes` (F3, F2), and every `Destination.reads` element has `.schema is Schema.DAR_USS` (F1). This test is also the justification for the `Plan`/`Step` union existing at all — if it is ever deleted, the union should be deleted with it.

**Gate — the existing `ty check --error all` hook.** Spike 4 showed this catches exactly the three shapes this design relies on: a wrong argument against a union alias, assignment to a frozen field, and an out-of-`Literal` discriminator. Adding a `Step` variant in a later slice must fail the gate until every `match` handles it, via `assert_never`.

**Tripwire for the restatement failure — reviewed at slice 2, not automated.** The diff that adds the second business entity must touch no file under `src/`. If it does, this decision has not held.

consequences.text: The blueprint's absolutes become executable rather than aspirational. F1 is `every Destination.reads element has schema.layer is Layer.DAR`; F3 is `every mapping's source relation is in das__staged`; the one-job-per-movement rule is the `Step` union's shape. A blueprint that states it "contains no exceptions and no pre-authorised bypass" but relies on memory to enforce them is enforced by memory; typed seams are what make the check writable.

Slice 2's cost is measurable and should be near zero under `src/`: a new entity, contract, mapping, measure and page are all artefact changes. That is the operational form of the blueprint's "a change costs about the same in year ten as in year one", and the tripwire that tells you the day it stops being true.

`ty --error all` becomes a load-bearing gate instead of a formality. Spike 4 observed it catching a frozen-field assignment, a wrong-union argument and an out-of-Literal discriminator on exactly this module shape, with "All checks passed!" and zero false positives on the good module.

The three silent-failure rules the spikes found get exactly one home each: `union_by_name => true` in `Landing.read_sql`, `extracted_on`/`extracted_at` derivation in `Load`, and close-before-daana in the `Warehouse` protocol. Each was observed to fail silently or with a misleading error, and each would otherwise be scattered across call sites.

Tool replaceability stops being a claim. dlt appears in one module, daana-cli in one, DuckDB behind one Protocol — so the blueprint's "every tool this system currently uses must be replaceable without invalidating a single line below" has a concrete surface area rather than a hope.

Neutral fixtures can stage what the real recording cannot: a column added in a second load (spike 1's silent-drop case), a reserved-word object name, a mixed-case source property, a nullable column. Testing those against Northwind would require fabricating the source anyway.

There are now two vocabularies in one repository, and a newcomer must learn `Relation`, `Landing`, `Step` and `Load` before they can read a five-line function that would have read as "open the orders parquet". The machinery vocabulary is a real onboarding tax, paid by every reader, and it is largest in slice 1 when there is least system to justify it.

`stage` now means three things — `das__staged`, `dab__stage`, and the USS `_stage` structural column. Renaming the plan unit to `Step` avoids a fourth, but it means code and artefacts use different words for adjacent ideas, and someone will read `_stage` as a pipeline step and write a wrong query.

Neutral fixtures cannot catch source-shaped bugs. An OData paging quirk, an `@odata.count` surprise, or a property whose casing only Northwind has will pass every machinery test and fail on the real source. The safety net is the data checks — which by conventions §6 land with the build that satisfies them, not before it — so every slice has a window in which the machinery is green and the data is wrong.

The lexical check will false-positive on business terms that are ordinary English or ordinary code words: `ORDER` lower-cased is `order`, and `NAME`, `STATUS`, `COUNT`, `GROUP` are all plausible model ids. That forces `tests/vocabulary_collisions.txt`, which is a small second artefact of exactly the kind the conventions' one-artefact principle dislikes, and which is a place a real violation can be parked and forgotten unless every addition to it is reviewed on its reason.

The `Plan`/`Step` union is dead weight unless the flow test is written against it. Five steps in fixed order is otherwise five function calls, and the corpus's warning lands squarely: "premature abstraction before patterns emerge adds overhead without benefit." This is a conditional cost that becomes a real one the moment someone deletes the test and keeps the types.

The emitter now owns SQL formatting responsibilities that hand-written SQL would not have. Spike 4 observed RF02 (unqualified references in multi-table selects) is the one rule sqlfluff cannot autofix, so the generator must table-qualify every reference itself, and it must emit `cast()` exclusively for CV11. That is generator complexity bought by the decision to generate.

Stack traces and log lines will contain no business word. A failure in `Unpack` reads as "no such relation in das__staged" unless the failing values are deliberately carried into every error message, which is discipline required on every error path rather than a property of the design.

Parsing `dab/model.yaml` is a standing restatement risk that no test fully closes. Every field the machinery reads is a field it could begin to interpret, and the line between "carries the definition" and "uses the definition" is a review judgement that must be made again at every slice.

consideredOptions: A typed machinery domain model with no business vocabulary under src/ or in tests, with neutral fixture systems held as data files
No domain model: plain dicts (or TypedDicts) parsed from YAML, with free functions over them
A typed model generated from dab/model.yaml, so the business model is mirrored as Python types in src/

result.contextAndProblem:
Slice 1 is the thinnest whole spine — one contract, one landed table, one staged view, one DAB entity, one transaction event, one count measure, one bridge with its peripheral and calendar, one question computed twice, one marimo page. Almost every part of it is a *generator*: something in Python reads a declaration and emits SQL or invokes a tool. That is where the two models meet, and where the confusion starts. `dab/model.yaml` is, by conventions §1.2, the only place the data is explained. But the USS generator has to read that file — it needs the entity's key, its attributes for the peripheral, and the event's date attribute for the calendar. The moment code reads the business model, the question "have we just written the business model twice?" becomes live, and it is not a rhetorical question: it is the difference between a machinery that works for any source and a machinery that works for Northwind.

What makes the obvious answer wrong here is that both obvious answers are wrong in opposite directions. The first obvious answer — parse the YAML into dicts, write the SQL, ship the slice — is defensible and the corpus even endorses it for systems this size: contract-driven-data-transformation says plainly that "for three source tables, just hand-write the SQL and move on with your life." But this repository has already made `ty --error all` a hard rule, and spike 4 observed what ty does with untyped dictionaries: `missing-type-argument` on a bare `dict`, and `d["k"]` "Inferred as `Unknown`". A gate that is a hard rule and checks nothing on the layer where every decision lives is worse than no gate, because it is trusted. The second obvious answer — mirror the model as Python types so the compiler knows what an ORDER is — is what a great many good systems do, and it buys real safety: a wrong attribute id becomes a check-time error instead of a run-time disagreement. It is also forbidden outright by conventions §5 and would put a second, drifting copy of the model inside `src/`.

The third thing that makes this hard is that slice 1 has exactly one of everything, so nothing in it can falsify an abstraction. Every type is unfalsified by induction, and the corpus names this failure mode by name: "Instead of undocumented transformations, you risk overly generic models lacking domain specificity", and "premature abstraction before patterns emerge adds overhead without benefit. Build a few implementations, discover commonalities, then abstract." A decision that mandates a typed domain model on the strength of one contract and one entity has to answer that warning honestly rather than quote past it, and it has to name which types it is *refusing* to build.

Fourth, the enforcement problem is genuinely unsolved by the documents as they stand. conventions §5 already makes "no data vocabulary anywhere under `src/` or in test code" a **hard rule** — so this ADR does not get to decide whether the rule exists, only whether anything makes it true. And the conventions document's own opening logic leaves a hole: "Where an off-the-shelf tool can already check a rule, the tool's configuration is the rule … everything else is checked by whoever — or whatever — reviews the change." No off-the-shelf tool checks this. So by the document's own construction, the rule falls to review — which is exactly where stop-being-naming-convention-police says conventions die: "People agree in the moment, then forget when they're actually writing code." Meanwhile the standard remedy, a hand-written denylist in a linter config, is precisely the second machine-readable copy the same document forbids because of drift.

Finally there are two smaller traps waiting in slice 1 specifically. The word `stage` already means three different things in this architecture — `das__staged`, `dab__stage`, and the USS `_stage` structural column that conventions §1.3 mandates — so a machinery type called `Stage` would make it four. And the marimo destination is Python, sits under `destinations/`, is matched by the ruff and ty pre-commit hooks, and *must* contain business words: axis labels, `_measure__…` column names. Conventions §5 scopes its rule to `src/` and test code, so the page is technically outside it, but the companion rule lists the artefact homes as "the YAML, SQL and Markdown artefacts" and does not contemplate a Python page. That ambiguity has to be resolved by this decision or it will be resolved by whoever writes the page first.
decisionDrivers: conventions.md §5 already makes "No data vocabulary anywhere under `src/` or in test code" a hard rule, and already prescribes the mechanism: "Test fixtures use neutral models held as data files, so the tests *prove* the machinery is generic rather than asserting it." This ADR decides what makes that true, not whether it is true.

The blog argues for an agent reading the convention document ("Documentation is enforcement"); conventions.md says tool-checkable rules are enforced by the tool's config and everything else by "whoever — or whatever — reviews the change". No spike tested any of the three tiers, and nothing anywhere gives a false-positive rate for a derived-denylist check. The implementer chooses, and will discover the real cost only after the first slice.

Whether the English-word collision allowlist is needed at all. That depends on the entity and attribute ids chosen for the Northwind model, which is a slice-1 modelling decision not yet made. If the ids are `ORDER`, `SHIP_COUNTRY` and `PLACED_ON`, then `order` alone forces the allowlist into existence.

Whether a neutral fixture's spine can run daana-cli in CI on every commit. Spike 2 proved deploy/execute works on DuckDB but did not measure wall-clock time, and it found that any other open connection to the file breaks execute with a misleading error. Spike 4's pytest ran with duckdb not installed at all ("Not tested: pytest against a real DuckDB file"). So whether the fixture tests exercise the full spine or stop at the daana seam is unresolved by evidence.

The syntax of `dab/uss.yaml`. The corpus places measures in three different layers (blog-synthesis records this as an explicit contradiction: "WHERE MEASURES/METRICS ARE DECLARED … Three placements") and no post shows the file. Whether a measure is declared by kind, by expression, or by nothing at all beyond its identity is a choice the implementer makes.

Whether `destinations/*.py` is linted and type-checked at all. Spike 4 flagged it as untested: "marimo cells are decorated functions in a generated file; `@app.cell` functions typically lack return annotations and would trip ANN201, and marimo rewrites the file on save which fights ruff format … likely a per-path ruff `per-file-ignores`." If it is checked, the interaction with the vocabulary rule needs the conventions clarification proposed above; if it is excluded, that exclusion is itself a decision.

Whether the USS generator reads `dab/model.yaml` or introspects the deployed `dab` schema. Spike 2 shows introspection is unreliable on DuckDB because the presentation views are table macros invisible to `information_schema`, but no spike tried reading the declaration and comparing the two for drift.

What `Relation.sql` should actually emit for DAB-side identifiers. Spike 2 observed DuckDB preserves entity-id casing and resolves case-insensitively, so both quoted and unquoted work; conventions §3 says identifiers crossing over from DAB are double-quoted while everything this repository creates is lower case and unquoted, and slice 1 sits on the boundary. Nothing settles which the generator emits.

Whether rendering the destination is a plan step or a CI action. Spike 3 established `marimo export thumbnail --execute` as the PR-acceptance mechanism, but whether the machinery owns marimo's lifecycle (a sixth `Step` kind) or leaves it to CI is undecided, and the answer changes the shape of `Plan`.

Whether `Question` stays a pair of SQL files. With one question, structure would be premature and would re-declare what `uss.yaml` owns; with several, the coverage argument from anatomy-of-business-question ("the questions become a specification") starts to bite. The trigger for revisiting is unresolved.

Whether `expected/` fixture artefacts should pin emitted SQL verbatim. Diffing generated SQL byte-for-byte makes every formatting change a test change; deriving expectations from the fixture's own declarations risks a tautological test that asserts the generator emitted what the model said. Neither the blog nor any spike addresses this, and it is the main way the fixture strategy can quietly stop catching bugs.

result.argument:
## Why the change log wins, and why it is the same decision as "DAB history is dated by extracted_at"

Start with the constraint that is already settled: DAB history is dated by `extracted_at`, which is `to_timestamp(cast(_dlt_load_id AS DOUBLE))`. That decision is only meaningful if a key can carry more than one `extracted_at` in the object DAB reads. If `das__staged` were latest-per-key, every row would carry exactly one `extracted_at` per key at any moment, daana's `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: extracted_at` would produce exactly one version per key per execute, and DAB's history would be a function of how often somebody ran the pipeline rather than a function of the data. Option A and the already-decided provenance rule are not two decisions; they are one decision looked at from two ends.

The property this buys is the one the blueprint calls reloadability and S2 calls non-volatility: "DAB and DAR must be rebuildable from DAS at any time without going back to the source." With a change log and `FULL_LOG`, dropping the whole DAB schema and re-executing reproduces byte-identical history, because every `eff_tmstp` is a value in a row and not a wall clock. Spike 2 finding 6 observed exactly this: with `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: das_load_ts`, "eff_tmstp in view_<entity>_hist IS the DAS load timestamp verbatim", and after appending a changed row with a later load timestamp, `view_CUSTOMER_hist` held both versions while `view_CUSTOMER` held only the new one. Spike 2 finding 8 observed the other half: `FULL_LOG` is idempotent against a source view holding two rows for the same key — runs 7 and 8 both left `CUSTOMER_desc` at 25 rows. The two spike findings together say that the log shape and daana's default strategy were built for each other.

The `__current` projection is not speculative and is not there because the blog has one. It is there because one of this system's own already-decided rules demands it: "each question is computed twice, from `das__staged` and from `dar__uss`, and the two must agree." Spike 1 measured what happens to that comparison over a log: two runs gave "240 rows / 120 distinct orders". `dar__uss` reflects DAB's current state, so the DAS-side computation of the same question must be over one row per key. Something has to deduplicate. The only question is where.

## The rejected options, at their strongest

**Option B — latest-per-key `das__staged`, history stays in `das__raw`** is the option with the best short-term ergonomics, and it should be argued seriously. Every question over DAS becomes a plain aggregate with no window function. daana's `FULL` strategy becomes safe, since spike 2 finding 10 confirmed `FULL` is correct against a one-row-per-key view. Nothing in the layer ever double-counts. And the claim that "history is not lost, it is in `das__raw`" is literally true: the parquet is append-only and every load is retained.

It fails on what "retained" has to mean. `das__raw` is one VARCHAR `payload` column. Recovering a historical version from it means re-applying the contract's casts by hand, outside the generator, which is the hand-written staging micro-decision the whole artefact exists to abolish — and it would be a *second*, divergent implementation of the same contract, so the drift the contract prevents comes back in the diagnostic path. Worse, the loss is silent and permanent in DAB rather than merely inconvenient. If two ingests land between two `daana-cli execute` runs, the intermediate version never becomes a `_desc` row, and no amount of re-executing recovers it, because the latest view no longer contains it. B3 ("every version retained, none overwritten") would then be satisfied only when the operator happened to run the DAB step at the right cadence. A time-variance guarantee that depends on scheduling is not a guarantee. B also cannot derive the log; A can derive both `__current` and, later, a per-load snapshot, from the log.

**Option C — log only, every consumer deduplicates** is the purest reading of S1. DAS captures and persists; a window function is arguably already an interpretation; one contract, one object, no naming argument. And it is cheap: a `QUALIFY` in a question is four lines.

It fails on the blog's central diagnosis, which is about the thirtieth file, not the first: "five different engineers have each made slightly different decisions… and the staging layer has quietly become a collection of undocumented micro-decisions." A dedup rule written by hand in each question is precisely such a micro-decision, and it is the *load-bearing* one, because it silently determines whether corrections win. It is also fatal to the parity check specifically: the DAS-side and DAR-side computations would embody two independently-written recency rules, so the check could agree for the wrong reason or disagree for a reason that is not a data defect. A parity check whose two sides do not share a definition of "current" is testing the person who wrote the SQL.

**Option D — the log in `das__staged`, the latest in a third schema** mirrors the blog's two target models as two datasets, which reads cleanly and makes the log-versus-current choice impossible to get wrong by mistyping a table name. It is the option I would take if the two projections had different owners or different refresh cadences. Here they do not. It costs a third schema in a two-schema layer that has already been decided (`das__raw`, `das__staged`), it breaks the convention that a contract's stem is "used in every schema of this layer" by putting the same stem in three schemas with three meanings, and it buys separation between two objects that are always generated together from one file and always in lockstep. Sibling objects in one schema express "same source, two projections" better than sibling schemas do.

**Option E — no contract in slice 1** deserves the most respect, because it is the blog's own advice against itself: "For three source tables, just hand-write the SQL and move on with your life… For thirty tables, the math flips." With one contract, the generator is more code than the SQL it emits, and every line of it is unpaid overhead against slice 1's actual question.

It fails on what slice 1 is for. A vertical slice exists to prove the *machinery* end to end, not to answer one question — the machinery is what gets widened, and conventions §5 forbids data vocabulary under `src/` precisely so that the machinery is proven generic rather than asserted to be. Hand-written staging for slice 1 means the second contract, not the thirtieth, is where the generator gets written, and it gets written against SQL that already encodes one table's accidents. It also means slice 1's data checks, its drift check and its parity check are all written against a hand-rolled shape and rewritten later. And it forfeits the property the ACID TEST is asking about at the exact moment it is cheapest to establish: "is your contract documentation that someone manually keeps in sync with custom SQL, or does it directly generate unpacking logic?" You cannot retrofit that; you can only start with it.

## Which projection gets the plain name

Given A, the plain name should be the log, and this is not a coin flip. Consider the two ways of pointing at the wrong object. Point DAB at `orders__current` when you meant the log: history silently degrades to one version per execute, nothing errors, and the loss is unrecoverable. Point a question at `orders` when you meant `__current`: the number is wrong by a factor of the load count, the parity check fails, and it is fixed by editing one line. The default must be the failure that is loud and recoverable. It is also what the layer's own principle says: S2 makes DAS the layer that retains everything, so the object carrying the layer's plain name should not be the one that drops rows.

## Two adaptations away from the blog that I want on the record

The blog composes a composite primary key into a `_pk` column with a `CONCAT` separator, and warns correctly that a missing separator merges `'A001'+'12'` with `'A0011'+'2'`. The work-before-the-answer case study reports the same class of bug found in production — "a silent identifier collision… the bug had been in the DAS for weeks, invisible because nothing downstream was looking at it." The right fix is not a better separator; it is not composing at all. `primary_keys` stays a *list*, and the list is consumed as a list — by `PARTITION BY` in `__current` and by the distinctness check — never concatenated. Identifier composition is a DAS→DAB boundary concern (integration-by-design puts the Owner+Type prefix in the reader cast), and daana's mapping YAML already takes `primary_keys` as a list (spike 2 finding 2). DAS therefore has no composed-key surface to get wrong.

The blog uses `SAFE_CAST` uniformly and lets `mode` drive only the test tier. In DuckDB there is a real choice between `cast` (raises) and `try_cast` (NULL), and I am choosing `try_cast` everywhere plus generated checks — deliberately, against the instinct that "strict" should mean "raises". A raising view is a view you cannot diagnose: the blog's own root-cause tree needs you to query the thing that is failing, and DuckDB's projection pushdown means a raising cast fires in some queries and not others, so the error is both fatal and non-deterministic in where it appears. `try_cast` keeps DAS readable at all times and moves strictness into three generated checks that are not optional: REQUIRED-null detection, cast-loss detection (raw text non-null but cast NULL — the blog's "EXTRACTION BUG" branch made mechanical), and payload-key drift (a key present in `payload` that no column declares — the "SOURCE CHANGED" branch). That is a strictly more informative gate than a raise, at the cost of only being loud when the gate runs, which I list as a consequence rather than hiding.

One further point about `mode` in this particular source: Northwind's `$metadata` marks thirteen of the fourteen Order properties nullable, so almost every column is `NULLABLE` and the null-detection tier guards only `OrderId`. It is tempting to declare `OrderDate` and `ShipCountry` REQUIRED because slice 1's question needs them. That would be a lie about the source, and S1/S5 forbid it: `mode` records what the *source* guarantees, not what we want. Our need for a non-null order month is a DAB and DAR requirement, and the check for it belongs there.

## Ordering, and why it must be the load time

`__current` orders by `extracted_at DESC`, never by a source timestamp such as `OrderDate`. The reason is the blog's stated requirement for the latest model: "If sources send incorrect data then corrections, 'latest' views automatically reflect the corrected state" — a correction arrives in a later load and must win even when the business date it carries is older. Load time is the only ordering under which that is true by construction, and it is the same value DAB dates its history by, so the two layers agree on what "later" means without either of them being told.

## 2. The type vocabulary and its DuckDB expressions

`P` is the `source_path`; the JSON path is `'$.' || P`. Spike 1 finding 15: `->>` yields VARCHAR, `->` yields JSON, both work directly on the VARCHAR `payload` column with an implicit cast.

| contract `type` | emitted expression | resulting DuckDB type |
|---|---|---|
| `STRING` | `raw.payload ->> '$.P'` | VARCHAR (no cast — `->>` is already VARCHAR) |
| `INTEGER` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS INTEGER)` | INTEGER |
| `BIGINT` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS BIGINT)` | BIGINT |
| `DECIMAL(p, s)` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS DECIMAL(p, s))` | DECIMAL(p,s) |
| `DOUBLE` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS DOUBLE)` | DOUBLE |
| `BOOLEAN` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS BOOLEAN)` | BOOLEAN |
| `DATE` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS DATE)` | DATE |
| `TIMESTAMP` | `try_cast(raw.payload ->> '$.P' AS TIMESTAMP)` | TIMESTAMP |

consequences.text: One artefact carries documentation, schema and transformation, so they cannot drift: adding a column to Northwind Orders is a five-line contract diff plus a regenerate, and the column's description, its cast, its null check and its warehouse COMMENT all move together. The blog's ACID TEST ('does it directly generate unpacking logic?') is passed by construction and is provable by a single machinery test.

Rebuild-from-DAS is deterministic. Because every eff_tmstp in DAB is a data value (extracted_at) rather than the wall clock of the run, dropping the whole DAB schema and re-executing reproduces byte-identical history. That is what makes daana's drop-and-redeploy upgrade path safe, and it is what blueprint S2 and the reloadability claim in design-of-analytical-systems actually require.

Corrections win automatically. Ordering __current by extracted_at DESC rather than by any source timestamp means a later load beats an earlier one even when it carries an older business date — the blog's stated requirement for a latest model — and it is the same ordering DAB uses, so the two layers cannot disagree about what 'later' means.

daana's FULL strategy becomes structurally unnecessary, so spike 2's silent-corruption bug is out of reach rather than merely avoided. FULL_LOG against the log is idempotent (spike 2 finding 8: 25 rows across runs 7 and 8) and produces exactly the history the build needs (findings 6 and 7).

The strict boundary is physical, not advisory: payload does not exist in das__staged, so no DAB mapping expression can reach past the contract into the raw JSON, and no consumer can accidentally depend on an undeclared source field.

das__staged.orders grows as loads x records with no compaction and no incremental predicate, and every consumer scans all of it. daana's FULL_LOG recomputes its true delta against the full log on every execute, so the DAB step is the first thing that slows down, and it slows down in proportion to how long the system has been running rather than to how much changed. Spike 1 explicitly did not measure this: 'Not tested at scale: 120 rows only... the cost of DuckDB scanning hundreds of small per-load parquet files was not measured.' Nothing in this design has a plan for compaction, and adding one later collides with S2's ban on rewriting.

Two objects per contract, and the more dangerous one has the shorter name. A question or a mapping that says das__staged.orders when it meant orders__current double-counts in exact proportion to the number of loads — and in a CI run that replays the fixture once, log and current are identical, so the mistake is invisible. The safety of this design rests on the CI protocol replaying twice, not on the schema. If someone 'speeds up CI' by dropping to one replay, the guard silently disappears.

__current means 'the latest version we ever received', not 'what the source has now'. A record deleted upstream stays in __current forever, and daana's FULL_LOG soft-delete never fires because the key never disappears from an append-only log. DAS as designed cannot express 'this key was absent from load N' at all; answering that needs a third projection nobody has designed. Anyone who reads 'FULL_LOG continues to soft-delete rows for source-row disappearance' and assumes deletes are handled will be wrong.

try_cast everywhere means a type violation is a NULL, not an error, until a check runs. Between two gate runs a REQUIRED column can be silently NULL all the way through DAB into a marimo page.
