result.contextAndProblem:
DAS is the only layer in this system that faces something nobody here controls. Everything above it — the DAB model, the generated USS, the marimo page — changes because we decided to change it. DAS changes because a third party changed something without telling us, and the blueprint's answer to that is two postures in one layer, not one: S3, "Forgiving ingestion, strict unpacking. Accept whatever arrives; enforce structure at the boundary out," with both halves justified by the same sentence — committing to a schema at ingest turns every upstream change into lost data, and enforcing nothing on the way out turns every upstream change into a silent one. The forgiving half is already settled: dlt lands the whole source record as one JSON column into hive-partitioned parquet, and spike 1 proved that works (`columns={"payload": {"data_type": "json"}}` produced exactly one `json` column with zero child tables even over nested objects and arrays). What is not settled is the strict half — what the artefact that enforces structure is, what it may say, and what SQL it turns into.

The hard part is not the mechanics. It is that the blueprint and the blog appear to contradict each other here, and the contradiction is registered in the synthesis: blueprint S1 says DAS is "Capture and persist only. No business logic, no interpretation, no enrichment," while four posts put unpacking, type casting, renaming and view generation inside DAS. The synthesis names it plainly: "Either the blueprint's DAS is only the landing zone (and staging is unlabelled), or the staging step violates a stated absolute." Both this repository's blueprint and the design-of-analytical-systems post resolve it the same way — DAS "often manifests as two physical layers: a raw landing zone and a staging area" — so the resolution is that `das__raw` is the capture, `das__staged` is the boundary out, and the contract's whole job is to enforce structure without adding meaning. That is only tenable if the contract is *structurally incapable* of expressing meaning, which makes the closed type vocabulary and the absence of any expression key load-bearing rather than stylistic.

Three specific things about this system make the obvious answers wrong. First, DAS here is append-only by construction and nothing ever rewrites it, so after two loads `das__staged` holds two rows per source record — spike 1 measured 240 rows for 120 distinct orders after two identical runs, and its own open questions list this as undesigned: "Does DAB want the full append history, or a latest-version view? This changes whether das__staged is a plain cast view or a QUALIFY/ROW_NUMBER view." Second, the consumer of `das__staged` is not a person writing SQL but daana-cli, and spike 2 found that its two candidate strategies have opposite requirements: `FULL_LOG` is idempotent against a multi-row-per-key source view, while `FULL` "silently inserts one extra duplicate row into `<entity>_desc` per execute, forever, and NONE of the presentation views show it." So the shape of `das__staged` decides, invisibly, whether the layer above it corrupts itself. Third, this system computes each question twice, once from `das__staged` and once from `dar__uss`, and requires the two to agree — which means `das__staged` must be able to answer a question at one-row-per-key, or the parity check becomes a comparison between a change log and a current state that can never agree.

There is a fourth pressure that cuts against building any of this. The blog that defines the contract is explicit that contracts are overhead at small scale: "For three source tables, just hand-write the SQL and move on with your life... For thirty tables, the math flips." Slice 1 has exactly one table. Every argument for a generator here has to survive the fact that its own primary source says not to build one yet.

Finally, the blog's contract shape was designed for Kafka into BigQuery, and two of its concrete mechanics do not survive the move. `SAFE_CAST` does not exist in DuckDB, so the contract's `mode` has to mean something different than it did; and the blog composes composite keys into a `_pk` column with a `CONCAT` separator, which the same corpus reports as the source of a real production bug — "a silent identifier collision... The bug had been in the DAS for weeks, invisible because nothing downstream was looking at it." What travels and what does not is therefore part of the decision, not a detail of it.

The timezone of dlt's {YYYY}-{MM}-{DD} layout placeholder versus to_timestamp's UTC. Spike 1 verified the placeholder names, not the midnight boundary. A load just either side of midnight UTC could land in a partition that disagrees with its own extracted_at. The generated check catches it after the fact; nothing prevents it.

Whether enable_dataset_name_normalization=False also stops TABLE-name normalisation. Spike 1 lists this as untested and it bites the moment a contract stem must come from an entity set like OrderDetails, which is exactly the next contract this system will need.

Whether `cast` (raises loudly, breaks readability, fires non-deterministically under projection pushdown) or `try_cast` (quiet, NULL, caught only by a check) is right for a REQUIRED column. This is a judgement about which failure the team prefers, not a fact either source settles; the blog uses SAFE_CAST uniformly and the blueprint's S3 argues the other way.

The word for the deduplicated projection. The blog says `latest`; this repository already spells the same idea `_is_current` in DAR (conventions §1.3). I have chosen `current` in both the contract and the object name so one idea has one word, but this is a coin flip and the only thing that matters is that the loser is never used again.

Whether the type vocabulary needs a format template. Every Northwind Edm.Date and Edm.Decimal cast cleanly in spike 1, so DATE/TIMESTAMP need no parse string today. The first source that sends a non-ISO date has no way to say so, and the choice is between a strptime template on the column and a new vocabulary entry per format — the blog's dictionary approach implies the latter.

Delete detection. DAS as designed cannot express 'this key was absent from load N', and neither the log nor the current view triggers daana's FULL_LOG soft-delete. Answering it needs a third projection over the most recent load only. Nobody has designed it and slice 1 does not need it, but the gap should be recorded before someone assumes soft-delete works.

Whether a record hash belongs in DAS. Spike 1 shows _dlt_id is not stable across loads, so content identity would have to be our own column; spike 2 shows daana already suppresses unchanged attributes, so DAB does not need it. That leaves 'did this load change anything at all?' as a full comparison rather than a hash compare — cheap now, expensive at volume.

Small-file and full-scan behaviour. Spike 1 measured 120 rows and explicitly did not measure DuckDB scanning hundreds of per-load parquet files, nor daana's FULL_LOG re-reading the whole log every execute. There is no compaction design and S2 makes the obvious one (rewriting files) illegal.

Contract granularity. The corpus contradicts itself — 'a data contract for each source' versus 'Each contract specifies a single source-to-staging transformation'. I have chosen one file per landed table because conventions §1.1 ties the file stem to the table name, but the ownership model in the blog is per-source and the two do not line up when one source has thirty entity sets.

How a source property whose name is a SQL reserved word, or contains a dot, or differs from another only by case, is represented. `source_path` has no quoting or escaping rule, and `target_name` is required to be the mechanical snake_case of it. DAR's precedent is to quote (dar__uss."order"), but nothing decides it for DAS.

Whether the CI protocol is a decision of this ADR or of the CI ADR. The safety of the two-object design depends entirely on CI replaying the fixture twice; with one replay the log and the current view are identical and none of this is tested. That protocol has to be owned somewhere explicitly.
result.recommendation: das__staged is the change log (one row per source record per load), and the same contract also generates a deduplicated das__staged.<table>__current beside it

## Why an event-grained bridge at all Start with the thing that is actually in dispute. The corpus argues for two DAR shapes and never reconciles them: `consumption-layer-generates-itself` says generate a USS, `why-we-built-daana` says "dimensional modeling remains the natural choice for the DAR layer", and `ai-assisted-data-engineering` describes a Kimball agent building "dimensions, facts, snapshots" with conformed dimensions. The blog-synthesis names this "the single biggest unresolved conflict". So the USS is not handed to us; it is chosen. It is chosen because of what slice 2 will look like. **Generated Kimball star per business process** is a genuinely strong option and deserves better than dismissal: each fact has one explicit grain, there are no NULL-heavy wide rows, `count(*)` on a fact means something, every BI tool on earth expects it, and blueprint R2 is satisfied natively because each product owns its star. What it costs is exactly the tax the blog itemises: the unit of work becomes one star per question, so cost scales with questions rather than with model changes; "which fact table" returns; and — decisively for this build — two processes measured on different dates cannot be put on one timeline without a conformed date dimension, which is shared structure and therefore the same R2 deviation we are already registering, only with more moving parts. We would pay D-0001's price and not get the thing D-0001 buys. **One Big Table per question** is the cheapest thing that could work and is the honest baseline for slice 1: one flat table, no joins, marimo reads it, done in an afternoon. It fails at question two. Every attribute is duplicated per question, every definition change touches N tables, and the blog's own projection diagram puts OBT downstream of the USS ("obt = flatten the row") precisely because generating it from the bridge is a selection rather than a build. Keep it as a future projection, not as the primary shape. **Hand-written SQL per question** is the option nobody argues for and everybody does. For slice 1 it is fifteen lines and strictly less code than a generator. It is rejected on blueprint R4 ("Nothing here is hand-written or hand-edited") and on the thing R4 protects: a hand-written consumption layer has no sliceability contract, so "which questions does this model answer" becomes faith rather than a lookup, and the blog's whole coverage claim evaporates. **Entity-grained bridge** (one row per order carrying `placed_on`, `shipped_on`, `required_on` as three date columns) deserves a real hearing because it makes cohort questions trivial and keeps `count(*)` meaningful. It fails the one requirement the post treats as load-bearing: "Instead of one row per entity instance, you make the bridge event-based: one row per measurement event, each carrying its own date... One calendar, every process." With three date columns you need three joins to one calendar or three calendars, and "what happened in Q1 across orders, shipments and returns" is back to stitching. Event grain is the thing that earns the single calendar. **Puppini-canonical bridge — Stage plus keys only, measures left on the peripherals** — is the strongest rejected option, and it is arguably more faithful to the book than the blog is. It keeps the bridge narrow and stable: adding a measure changes a peripheral, not the structure every consumer reads. The blog explicitly departs from it ("It holds all the relations and all the measures in one place"; `SUM(b._measure__order_line__revenue) FROM _bridge b`), but "the blog said so" is not an argument. The argument is that a measure on a peripheral sits at *entity* grain, and an entity-grained measure cannot be dated by two different events. Revenue measured at placement and revenue measured at shipment are two numbers on two dates; on a peripheral there is one row and one place to put it. Once the bridge is event-grained, measures must live on the event row. Measures-on-bridge is not a stylistic preference, it is forced by the grain. ## 1. Fan-out: what propagates, and what the diagram already told us The post's sentence and the post's diagram disagree, and the disagreement is the whole problem. The sentence: "follow the relationships that go from many to one and inherit the keys **and measures** of everything you reach." The diagram immediately below it: walking n:1 from three lines to one order and summing the order's revenue gives 100, "counted once"; copying the order's 100 down onto the three lines gives 300, "fan-out, ×3". But copying the parent's measure onto every child row *is* the second picture. If "inherit the measures" meant "copy the values down", the safe walk would produce the unsafe number. The reading that makes the post coherent — and the decision here — is that **keys propagate and measure values do not propagate at all**. Precisely, for a stage rooted at entity E: - `E_key` is present and non-null. This is the row's own identity. - For every entity P reachable from E by a path made only of many-to-one edges, `P_key` is present, obtained by LEFT JOIN along the relationship views, and nullable where the relationship is optional. This is the downward propagation. - For any entity C on the one-to-many side of E, `C_key` is **never** present. There is no upward propagation; that direction is the fan. - Measures declared on (E, event) carry their value. **Every other measure column in the bridge is a typed NULL on these rows.** What a child inherits from a parent is therefore not the parent's measure but the parent's *dimensionality*: because the order-line rows carry `customer_key`, the order line's own measures become sliceable by customer attributes. Sliceability is the transitive closure of key inheritance. Measure values have no closure. That single sentence is the whole content of "cascading inheritance", stated so it cannot be implemented wrongly, and it is what makes the sliceability contract mechanically derivable: measure *m* owned by stage *S* is sliceable by key *k* exactly when *S* populates *k*. Nothing else needs deciding. The corollary, and it is not free: a *parent's* measure is not sliceable by a *child's* attribute. `placed_orders_count` cannot be broken down by product, ever, because the order-placed stage has no `product_key` and must not acquire one. The blog admits this class ("distinct counts across the wrong grain... you still have to think") without saying it out loud. The sliceability contract has to publish the absence, or the first analyst to want orders-by-product will discover it by getting a wrong number somewhere else. **The tests that prove it.** Three, and they are generated, not hand-written: *Ownership.* For each measure column, `count(*) WHERE IS NOT NULL AND (_stage, _event) <> (owner)` must be 0. This is the direct mechanical assertion that no measure value has propagated anywhere. It fails the day somebody "helpfully" fills a NULL. *Grain.* Each stage's row count equals the count of rows in its driving DAB view after the event-date filter and the version collapse. A LEFT JOIN along a relationship that turned out not to be many-to-one shows up here as a row count that is too high — which is the fan-out arriving through the key path rather than the measure path. *Join safety.* `_bridge LEFT JOIN USING (_key)` must have exactly the row count of `_bridge`, and every peripheral must satisfy `count(*) = count(DISTINCT _key)`. This is where a Kimball fan trap would actually materialise — at the consumer's join, not in the bridge — and it is why the peripheral is defined as one row per key rather than as the history view. The already-decided "computed twice from `das__staged` and from `dar__uss`" check sits on top of these and catches everything else. It is worth being honest about its limit: both computations express the same version-collapse rule, so it does not independently validate that rule. What it does validate is that the DAB mapping, the walk, the event filter and the peripheral join together reproduce a number derived from parquet the DAB layer never touched. That is worth a great deal, and it is not everything. ## 2. History: two stage kinds, one source view daana gives us `view_` (current, one row per key), `view__hist` (one row per value-run, dated `eff_tmstp`), and `view___`. The temptation is to read `view_` for events and `view__hist` for history. That is wrong in a way that only shows up later, for two reasons. First, `view_` carries no `eff_tmstp` and no `ver_tmstp` — spike 2 observed its column list as `ORDER_key` plus attributes only. A bridge built on it has no per-row provenance at all, which fails blueprint R5 and leaves no way to answer "which extraction produced this row". Second, and more important: by the earlier decision, DAB history is dated by `extracted_at`. So `eff_tmstp` is *when we saw it*, not *when it was true*. The `_hist` timeline is an **observation** timeline. That single fact settles the shape of the answer. A question about something that *happened* is dated by a business date attribute the model declares. A question about a state *as observed* is dated by `eff_tmstp`. uss:

## `dar__uss._bridge` — the complete column contract

| Column | Type | Null | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `_stage` | VARCHAR | no | the entity this row is a row *of*; equals the name of the peripheral whose key is guaranteed non-null here (`order`) |
| `_event` | VARCHAR | no | the event identifier, lower-cased (`placed`, `shipped`, `observed`) |
| `_event_date` | DATE | no | the date of the measurement event; joins `_calendar.date_key` |
| `_is_current` | BOOLEAN | no | TRUE if this row reflects the entity version currently in effect; always TRUE on a transaction stage |

| `<entity>_key` | VARCHAR | own key: no; inherited: yes | one column per entity populated by at least one stage. Own key non-null; parent keys inherited along many-to-one edges; child keys never present |
| `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` | BIGINT for `count`, DECIMAL(28,8) for `sum` of a numeric attribute | non-null only on the owning stage | one column per declared measure. Non-owning branches emit `cast(NULL AS <T>)` |

| Column | Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `date_key` | DATE | `1996-07-04` |
| `year_number` | INTEGER | `1996` |
| `quarter_of_year` | INTEGER | `3` |

| `quarter_start` | DATE | `1996-07-01` |

| `quarter_label` | VARCHAR | `1996-Q3` |

## Worked example — the single transaction stage, house style

`dar/uss/_bridge.sql` (verified: executes on duckdb 1.5.5, lints clean under the repo's `.sqlfluff`)

```sql
-- Generated by `uv run adss dar generate`. Do not edit; edit dab/uss.yaml and regenerate.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss._bridge AS
WITH order_placed AS (
    SELECT
        o."ORDER_key" AS order_key,
        o.eff_tmstp AS observed_at,
        cast(o."PLACED_ON" AS DATE) AS event_date
    FROM dab."view_ORDER_hist" AS o
    WHERE o."PLACED_ON" IS NOT NULL
    QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
        PARTITION BY o."ORDER_key"
        ORDER BY o.eff_tmstp DESC
    ) = 1
)

SELECT
    'order' AS _stage,
    'placed' AS _event,
    op.event_date AS _event_date,
    TRUE AS _is_current,
    op.observed_at AS _observed_at,
    op.order_key AS order_key,
    cast(1 AS BIGINT) AS _measure__order__placed_orders_count
FROM order_placed AS op;
```

A second stage is a second CTE plus a `UNION ALL` branch that emits `cast(NULL AS BIGINT) AS _measure__order__placed_orders_count` and `cast(1 AS BIGINT) AS _measure__order__shipped_orders_count`. Verified end to end on three synthetic hist rows: placed total 2, shipped total 1, `count(*)` 3, ownership violations 0 — the unshipped order correctly has no shipment row.

## `dar/uss/_calendar.sql`

```sql

WITH bounds AS (
    SELECT
        min(b._event_date) AS first_date,
        max(b._event_date) AS last_date
    FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
),

calendar_day AS (
    SELECT
        cast(d.day_ts AS DATE) AS date_key
    FROM bounds AS bo,
        range(bo.first_date, bo.last_date + INTERVAL 1 DAY, INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS d (day_ts)

    cd.date_key AS date_key,
    cast(year(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS year_number,
    cast(quarter(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS quarter_of_year,
    cast(month(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS month_of_year,
    cast(day(cd.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS day_of_month,
    cast(date_trunc('year', cd.date_key) AS DATE) AS year_start,
    cast(date_trunc('quarter', cd.date_key) AS DATE) AS quarter_start,
    cast(date_trunc('month', cd.date_key) AS DATE) AS month_start,
    strftime(cd.date_key, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(cd.date_key) AS VARCHAR) AS quarter_label,
    strftime(cd.date_key, '%Y-%m') AS month_label
FROM calendar_day AS cd;
```

Business validity intervals do not exist in this warehouse unless a business date attribute carries them. That means a question about something that *happened* and a question about a state *as observed* are dated by two entirely different clocks, and a bridge that conflates them will answer "how many orders were placed in July 1996" with a number that moves whenever we reload.

**Why the question directory wins.**

The deciding constraint is not aesthetic, it is mechanical, and it was observed rather than assumed. SPIKE 4's working pre-commit configuration binds sqlfluff with `types: [sql]` and `templater = raw`. A `.sql` file under `questions/` is linted by the same gate, with the same `.sqlfluff`, as generated DAR output — which is exactly what conventions §3 demands ("generated and hand-written SQL have to be indistinguishable to a reviewer", and "SQL that lives in a Python string is written to a file so the same linter sees it"). SQL in a fenced block inside `question.md` is invisible to that hook. Option 2 would have to reintroduce the linter through a bespoke extraction step, which is a second place where the SQL rules live, and conventions opens by refusing exactly that ("A convention that exists both as prose and as a linter config exists twice"). The directory gets the linting for free and pays only one price: two artefacts that can drift. That price is refundable, because the front matter names both files and `adss questions check` fails on a named file that is missing and on a `.sql` file under `questions/` that no question names — an orphan query cannot exist.

The second reason is the layering of what a commit may contain. Conventions §6 says data checks "assert what the built warehouse contains and land in the same commit as the build that satisfies them", while §7 says every commit passes the whole suite on its own. If the queries live inside `question.md`, the question cannot land before the warehouse does, because landing it would land two failing checks. Separating them lets commit one carry the question, `expected.csv` and `status: draft` — the specification — and lets each query land with the layer it interrogates. The write-the-staged-query-first ordering that makes independence credible then falls out of rules that already exist, instead of needing a new rule nobody can enforce.

**Why not generate both queries (option 3).** This is the option most consistent with the blog's surface rhetoric, and it is the one I most want to reject clearly, because it is seductive. consumption-layer-generates-itself is emphatic: "stop writing the artifact, declare the model and generate the artifact", and the sliceability contract is supposed to turn "Can I break revenue down by region" into "a lookup". Generating `uss.sql` from the front matter is genuinely right and I expect this build to arrive there — the front matter I have designed is already a metric declaration in all but name, and the day the generator emits `uss.sql` from it, nothing in the question file changes. What must never be generated is the *staged* query. To generate a das__staged query the generator would have to read the DAS→DAB mapping and re-express it in SQL. That is a second implementation of integration, which breaks blueprint B8 ("Meaning is defined exactly once, here") and the one-job-per-movement rule, and — fatally — it destroys the test. Two artefacts produced by one generator from one declaration share every failure mode that matters. Their agreement would prove that the generator is deterministic, which nobody doubted. The blueprint already names this trap: "Generation guarantees consistency, not correctness... a system that enforces coherent structure over incoherent definitions produces coherent-looking incoherence — which is more dangerous than visible mess, because it is trusted." A generated agreement check is that sentence made executable.

**Why not the pytest suite alone (option 4).** This is the cheapest option and it is not a strawman: it is what most competent teams do, the checks would be real, and the vertical slice would still work. It fails on two counts. First, conventions §5 forbids data vocabulary anywhere under `src/` or in test code — `ORDER`, `ship_country` and `placed_orders_count` may not appear in a test module, so the SQL and its expectations have to live outside the suite anyway, and option 4 collapses into option 1 with the metadata thrown away. Second, and more importantly, it discards the artefact that anatomy-of-business-question exists to produce. The post's whole argument is that the value is in the Stage 0 → Stage 3 transit: "Stage 3 - The question with definitions: The precise question, plus explicit definitions for every term that could be ambiguous." A test asserts the answer; it does not record the persona, the W's, the exclusions, or what the business will do with it. And blueprint R5 requires "What was delivered, to whom, and when is recorded... including the definitions that produced it". A pytest module records none of that. If the question lives in a PR title, it dies when the PR is merged — which is precisely the "copy-pasted, long query" failure Calle describes in the-work-before-the-answer: "someone would send me a screenshot or link to a dashboard I had never seen before, using a copy-pasted, long query".

**Why not the marimo page as the question (option 5).** It has the best property of all: zero drift, because prose, queries, answer and chart are one file that is executed. If marimo notebooks were plain, lintable, diffable artefacts I would take it. They are not. SPIKE 4's open questions flag exactly this: "marimo cells are decorated functions in a generated file; `@app.cell` functions typically lack return annotations and would trip ANN201, and marimo rewrites the file on save which fights ruff format." A page is also a *destination* — the one thing blueprint F1 says may read only DAR — and putting the DAS-reading query inside it makes the F1 breach permanent and load-bearing rather than confined to a test path. Rejected, but its good idea is kept: the page carries no SQL of its own and executes the question's `uss.sql` verbatim, so the page cannot drift from the checked answer.

**On the two queries, honestly.** The mechanism that makes the das__staged query independent is not that a different person wrote it; it is that it is *forbidden from touching the other's inputs*. `staged.sql` may contain no `dab` or `dar__` token and `uss.sql` may contain no `das__` token — a grep, not a discipline. That forces the staged query to re-derive the month from a cast date (`date_trunc('month', o.order_date)`) and the count from `count(*)` over a self-deduplicated set, where the USS query gets its month from a generated calendar table and its count from `sum(_measure__order__placed_orders_count)` over an event-filtered bridge. Different inputs, different mechanism, different arithmetic.

That still leaves the real risk: two queries written on the same afternoon by the same author, converging because the author wants green. The blog does not do it this way. the-work-before-the-answer's recommendation is "iterate against existing trusted reports where possible", and ai-assisted-data-engineering's Validation Agent's first mode is "platform comparison" — both compare against an *external* reference. So the honest design is a tripod, not a pair: `expected.csv` is pinned at question time from the recorded fixture by a method named in the front matter, and both queries are compared to it as well as to each other. Because the source is recorded once and replayed, the expected answer is a stable, knowable fact, and `@odata.count = 830` is a number the source itself produced (SPIKE 1 observed it). The residual risk is that a red golden file gets regenerated rather than investigated. Conventions §6 forbids that in words; design-of-analytical-systems tells us words erode ("Discipline depends on attention, attention is scarce under deadline pressure"). I will not pretend otherwise: this is the weakest leg and the reason `expected_method` is a required key rather than a comment.

**On what the check does and does not catch.** It catches the class of bug that the blog says cost six weeks: "a silent identifier collision I didn't find until I started building a thin DAR prototype... Two records that should have been distinct were being merged into one... The bug had been in the DAS for weeks, invisible because nothing downstream was looking at it." Two orders merged into one is a count difference. It also catches fan-out in the bridge, the wrong date column wired to an event, rows lost at a mapping boundary, and calendar gaps. It does not catch anything upstream of the fork. Both queries read the same landed parquet, so SPIKE 1's observed silent column loss — "a plain read_parquet glob over an append-only lake SILENTLY DROPS columns added in later loads — no error, just missing data" — or a dropped OData page yields two agreeing wrong answers and a green check. And SPIKE 2 supplies the sharpest counter-example available: under `ingestion_strategy: FULL` against a multi-row source view, `<entity>_desc` grew by one row per execute, "22 -> 23 -> 24 -> 25", while "view_CUSTOMER stayed at 3 rows and view_CUSTOMER_hist at 4 rows throughout — the corruption never surfaces in the views." A question check that reads only views would have been green for the entire life of that bug. Green means the layers agree, not that the number is right, and the question file must say so in its own prose or it will be read as the latter.

**On the F1 problem.** `staged.sql` reads DAS. Blueprint F1 says "Analytical usage reads only DAR", and the blueprint contains "no exceptions and no pre-authorised bypass". I recommend clarifying conventions rather than registering a deviation, on the ground that F1 is aimed at *consumption*, and its stated reason is invisible dependency: "The dependency is invisible until something breaks." A check query is the most visible dependency it is possible to write — it exists in order to break — and conventions §9 puts "Clarify this page" first precisely for "a case the rule was not aimed at". The clarification must be narrow and mechanical, not a licence: a DAS-reading query may exist only inside a question directory, may be executed only by the check runner, and no file under `destinations/` may mention `das__` or `dab`. If a reviewer rejects that reading, the fallback is not to abandon the check but to register D-0002 — rule F1, why (correctness cannot be proved from inside one implementation), cost (a permanent shape dependency on the layer that must stay free to change), exit condition (a trusted external report exists for the question). Both fields are answerable, so the deviation is legitimate if it is wanted. What is not acceptable is leaving it unexamined.

**On lifecycle.** Step 5 produces validation, refinement or pivot. Refinement and pivot both change the question sentence, and blueprint R5 says an answer someone acted on must be reconstructable "including the definitions that produced it". Editing a question in place destroys that, so a changed sentence forks a new question and the old one becomes `superseded`, keeping its queries and its answer — the same rule conventions §8 already applies to ADRs ("superseded by a new file rather than edited"). The bright line is the sentence: prose, owner, and the lifecycle log may be edited in place; the `question:` string may not. The cost is proliferation, and I name it below rather than hiding it.

`staged.sql` reads `das__staged.orders` and nothing else. It picks the current version of each
order by `extracted_at`, drops orders with no order date, truncates the date to a month and
counts rows. It never mentions `dab` or `dar__`.

`uss.sql` reads `dar__uss` and nothing else. It filters the bridge to the `placed` event, gets
its month by joining the generated calendar and its count by summing the measure column. It
never mentions `das__`.

Both are compared to `expected.csv`, which was pinned before either was written. Agreement
proves the layers do not disagree. It does not prove the number is right: both read the same
landed parquet, so an extraction fault produces two agreeing wrong answers.

See `expected.csv`; rendered at `destinations/q_01_orders_per_order_month_and_ship_country.py`.

## `staged.sql`

```sql
WITH current_order AS (
    SELECT
        o.order_id AS order_id,
        o.order_date AS order_date,
        o.ship_country AS ship_country
    FROM das__staged.orders AS o
    QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
        PARTITION BY o.order_id
        ORDER BY o.extracted_at DESC
    ) = 1
),

placed_order AS (
    SELECT
        co.order_id AS order_id,
        cast(date_trunc('month', co.order_date) AS DATE) AS month_start,
        co.ship_country AS order_ship_country
    FROM current_order AS co
    WHERE co.order_date IS NOT NULL
)

SELECT
    po.month_start AS month_start,
    po.order_ship_country AS order_ship_country,
    cast(count(*) AS BIGINT) AS placed_orders_count
FROM placed_order AS po
GROUP BY po.month_start, po.order_ship_country
ORDER BY po.month_start, po.order_ship_country;
```

The dedupe is not decoration: SPIKE 1 observed two identical runs producing "240 rows for 120 distinct orders". The `QUALIFY` runs before the null filter so that "current version" is decided first and the exclusion second — the reverse order would silently pick the latest *non-null* version.

## `uss.sql`

```sql
SELECT
    c.month_start AS month_start,
    o.order_ship_country AS order_ship_country,
    cast(sum(b._measure__order__placed_orders_count) AS BIGINT) AS placed_orders_count
FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS c ON b._event_date = c.date_key
INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key
WHERE b._stage = 'order' AND b._event = 'placed' AND b._is_current
GROUP BY c.month_start, o.order_ship_country
ORDER BY c.month_start, o.order_ship_country;
```

`cast(... AS BIGINT)` is required, not cosmetic: SPIKE 3 observed "DuckDB DECIMAL columns arrive as polars `decimal[38,0]` and altair cannot encode them", and this statement is what the page runs.

consequences.text: One artefact is simultaneously the specification, the acceptance test and the delivery record. Blueprint R5 ("What was delivered, to whom, and when is recorded... including the definitions that produced it") is satisfied by the thing the team was going to write anyway, rather than by a separate register that would drift.

Three of the four failure modes anatomy-of-business-question names become mechanical rather than cultural: a compound question cannot be expressed because the schema admits exactly one measure and one aggregation; a missing time dimension cannot be expressed because time_grain and time_window are required; an undefined term cannot pass because every ref must resolve. Only the missing question mark is a string check, and it is trivially one.

Definitions cannot be restated. The question references, the CLI resolves at read time, and no definition text is ever copied into a question file. Conventions §1.2 and blueprint B8 hold by construction rather than by review vigilance.

The agreement check catches the exact bug class the corpus reports as most expensive: "a silent identifier collision I didn't find until I started building a thin DAR prototype... The bug had been in the DAS for weeks, invisible because nothing downstream was looking at it." Two orders merged into one is a count difference and it goes red.

The marimo page executes the question's own uss.sql, so the number on the page is the number the check verified. The classic "the dashboard says something else" gap is closed by construction, and by a grep rather than a habit.

A question that needs an undefined term is expressible: it sits at status draft with the missing refs in blocked_by, CI holds it to exactly that list in both directions, and the slice does not open. Step 2's gap discovery — "we don't have a product_category attribute. Back to the business or flag it" — becomes a checked state instead of a conversation someone remembers.

staged.sql is a permanent, deliberate consumer dependency on das__staged's physical shape, in the layer whose whole purpose is to be free to change, and the count of such dependencies grows by one every slice and never shrinks. Renaming or retyping one contract column breaks N question checks at once, and the person who pays is whoever is absorbing the source change — precisely the cost blueprint F1 exists to prevent. It also puts source vocabulary (order_date, ship_country) into an artefact that lives outside DAS.

Two queries can be made to agree without either being right, and the cheapest way to clear a red check is to edit whichever query looks wrong. The pinned expected.csv reduces this but relocates it: the cheapest way to clear a red golden file is to regenerate it. Conventions §6 forbids both in words, and design-of-analytical-systems says words erode — "Discipline depends on attention, attention is scarce under deadline pressure." Nothing in this design makes that impossible; the mtime heuristic only makes it visible.

Both queries fork below DAS, so the whole of ingestion and unpacking is outside what agreement can test. SPIKE 1 observed a plain read_parquet glob silently dropping columns added in later loads — "no error, just missing data" — and a dropped OData page has the same shape. In both cases the two queries agree on a wrong number and CI reports green with maximum confidence. The check will be read as "the answer is right" when it only says "the layers do not disagree", and no amount of prose in the question file fully prevents that misreading.

There is an observed bug class it demonstrably misses. SPIKE 2 found that ingestion_strategy: FULL against a multi-row source view added one duplicate row to <entity>_desc per execute — "22 -> 23 -> 24 -> 25" — while "view_CUSTOMER stayed at 3 rows and view_CUSTOMER_hist at 4 rows throughout — the corruption never surfaces in the views." A question check reads the views. It would have been green for the entire life of that bug, and would have been cited as evidence the warehouse was sound.

Supersede-don't-edit means question files accumulate and are never deleted. A refinement as small as adding one dimension forks a near-duplicate directory with its own two queries and its own pinned expectation, so after twenty slices there are more question files than live questions, every one still executing on every CI run. questions/README.md becomes the only way to see the live set, and an index is exactly the kind of second surface this repository's conventions distrust.

The ceremony is heavier than the question on slice 1, and the methodology says so about itself: "If you have three tables and one stakeholder, skip the methodology and just build the dashboard." This build has one source, one entity and no real business. The front matter's persona, W's and acceptance scope will be written by the person who also writes the queries, which is the same tribal knowledge the artefact is supposed to displace, now with a schema around it. The payoff is real but arrives around slice five, and until then the file is a cost paid on faith.

Running the checks holds a DuckDB connection, and SPIKE 2 observed that any other open connection — "read-write OR READ-ONLY" — makes daana-cli execute fail with the misleading message "daana framework is not installed on the remote database". So question checks must be strictly sequenced after the DAB step, and a developer who leaves the marimo page open will see an error that tells them to reinstall the framework. Every slice inherits that operational trap.

result.contextAndProblem:
Conventions §7 already fixes the unit of delivery — "One business question per slice; one branch per slice" — and calls it a hard rule whose reason is that "The unit of delivery is an answered question, not a file." What it does not fix is what a question *is* as an artefact, where it lives, what it must carry, or how anyone knows the answer it delivers is right. That is what makes this hard: the blueprint gives four qualities and three flow rules, but says nothing at all about questions, and the two posts that do define a question define it as a *conversation output* — a whiteboard, a prioritised list, a workshop artefact — not as a versioned file that a CI job can hold to account.

The specific difficulty in *this* system is that the obvious answer — write the question in the ADR or the PR, put the assertions in the test suite — is blocked by three rules that were decided for other reasons and collide here. Conventions §5 forbids data vocabulary "anywhere under `src/` or in test code", so `ORDER`, `ship_country` and `placed_orders_count` may not appear in a pytest module; the vocabulary has to live in a YAML, SQL or Markdown artefact. Conventions §6 splits testing in two — machinery is test-first, but "Data checks are not written against a stub. They assert what the built warehouse contains and land in the same commit as the build that satisfies them" — so a question's assertions cannot all land in one commit. And conventions §3 requires that "SQL that lives in a Python string is written to a file so the same linter sees it", which SPIKE 4 makes concrete: the working pre-commit hook binds sqlfluff to `types: [sql]`, so SQL that is not in a `.sql` file is unlinted, whatever the prose says.

The second difficulty is definitional. Conventions §1.2 makes `dab/model.yaml` the sole home of meaning: "Every entity, attribute and relationship has a `definition` in business language, and that is the **only** place the data is explained. Everything else — contracts, questions, the generated layer, the app — references these." So a question may not carry definitions; it must carry pointers, and something must prove the pointers land. But the four-level Definition hierarchy that definitions-for-integration requires — Concept, Characteristic, Domain, Value, each "its own Concept requiring its own Definition" — has only two slots in the model: entity and attribute. Domains and Values have nowhere to live except free text, and the blog explicitly defers the fix ("we explore how this integration discipline translates to declarative architectures... in Part 3"), which is not in the corpus. Slice 1 walks straight into this: "ship country" is a closed Domain in principle and free source text in fact, and "order month" is a time grain that blueprint B5 forbids DAB from holding at all ("No aggregation, no bucketing, no pre-rollup"), so its definition cannot live where all definitions are supposed to live.

The third difficulty is that the two-query check, taken at face value, is weaker than it looks and stronger than the corpus actually supports. Nothing in the blog proposes comparing two implementations of your own system against each other. What it proposes is comparison against something external: "iterate against existing trusted reports where possible", and a Validation Agent whose first mode is "platform comparison". Comparing new-against-new is a self-consistency test, and the blueprint has already named the failure it cannot see — "a system that enforces coherent structure over incoherent definitions produces coherent-looking incoherence, which is more dangerous than visible mess, because it is trusted." Worse, the spikes supply a concrete bug the check provably misses: SPIKE 2 watched `<entity>_desc` grow by one duplicate row per execute while every presentation view stayed stable, "the corruption never surfaces in the views." So the design has to be honest about what green means, and has to find a third reference point if it wants to claim more than agreement.

Finally there is a flow-rule collision that cannot be dodged. One of the two queries reads `das__staged`, and blueprint F1 says "Analytical usage reads only DAR", in a document that states "This document contains no exceptions and no pre-authorised bypass." Either a check query is not analytical usage — a clarification — or it is, and it needs deviation D-0002 with a costed exit condition. Deciding that is part of deciding this, because the deviations register exists precisely so that "an unregistered exception is indistinguishable from a mistake."
decisionDrivers: The unit of delivery is already fixed by conventions §7 ("One business question per slice"); this decision must give that unit a physical form, not re-argue it.

A question must be answerable without conversation: measure, dimensions, aggregation, time grain, time window, persona, the W's and the action, per anatomy-of-business-question's Stage 3 and the W framework.
Meaning has exactly one home (conventions §1.2, blueprint B8), so a question references definitions and never restates them — and something mechanical must prove every reference resolves.

Correctness cannot be proved from inside one implementation; the blueprint concedes that generation buys consistency, not correctness, so the answer must be computed twice by genuinely different means.
sqlfluff sees only .sql files (SPIKE 4's working hook binds types: [sql]), and conventions §3 requires hand-written and generated SQL to be indistinguishable to the same linter.
Conventions §5 bars data vocabulary from src/ and from test code, so question vocabulary must live in YAML/SQL/Markdown artefacts and the runner must be generic over them.
Conventions §6 forces machinery to be test-first and data checks to land with the build that satisfies them, so a question's parts land in different commits of the same slice.
Blueprint R5 requires that what was delivered, to whom and when is recorded, including the definitions that produced it — so a question's history must survive its own revision.
The corpus's own validation practice compares against an external reference ("iterate against existing trusted reports"), not against a second copy of the same system.
Blueprint F1 ("Analytical usage reads only DAR") is directly in tension with a query that reads das__staged, and the blueprint pre-authorises no bypasses.

This ADR recommends the clarification and gives the deviation's four fields in case a reviewer disagrees; the decision is a judgement about what "analytical usage" means and it is not settled by anything written down.

Whether questions/README.md is generated from the question files or hand-maintained. Generated is consistent with the repository's distrust of second surfaces; hand-maintained is one fewer piece of machinery. Nothing decides it.

Whether the immutable-sentence rule can be enforced mechanically. CI can compare a question's sentence to its own history, but only if history is available to the check; on a fresh clone in CI it is, on a shallow one it is not. Until that is settled it is a review rule, not a check.

A small internal inconsistency the implementer must close: the observed lint sample writes `o."SHIP_COUNTRY" AS order_ship_country`, which conventions §1.3 ("the lower-cased attribute identifier, unchanged") forbids. This design assumes the DAB attribute is ORDER_SHIP_COUNTRY so the DAR column is mechanically derivable — the reference-coverage check depends on that being true, and it should be confirmed before the check is written.

result.argument:
**Why the acquisition question has only one honest answer: the binary has no version.**

`daana-cli -v` prints `daana-cli version nightly, commit 113d5a6a77c123679656a9c769c6b88123341f36, built at 2026-09-04T22:13:46Z`. There is no semantic version to depend on. You cannot write "requires daana-cli >= 0.7.0" and have it mean anything, because the artefact does not claim to be 0.7.0. It claims to be *nightly*, which is a name for "whatever was on the branch that night". Every acquisition option therefore has to answer the same question — *which bytes* — and only two mechanisms can answer it: carry the bytes, or record their hash. The `.sha256` sitting beside the binary makes the second one free, and I verified it resolves against the copy present here (`492ddf86ab3361104f503a6e0cc9ce412ec6dfbcc744e7c30ae23eb0ccc739d3`, `sha256sum` agrees). That single fact — *no version exists, only content* — is what makes "content-pinned manifest" not one option among several but the shape any workable option has to take. The remaining choice is only *where the bytes live between commits*, and that is a much smaller question than it looks.

**Vendoring it via LFS, argued properly.** This is the option with the best failure mode and I want to be fair to it. `git clone` gives you a working system with no second step, no cache to warm, no network call at build time that can fail on a Tuesday. The pin is the repository itself; the review of an engine upgrade is a diff of an LFS pointer, which is exactly as reviewable as a hash in a manifest. There is no "it worked on my machine" because there is only one machine's worth of bytes. Against a 174 MB object the cost is not disk — disk is free — it is three other things. First, GitHub's LFS bandwidth is metered and `actions/checkout` with `lfs: true` pulls the object on **every** run; at 174 MB the free tier is exhausted in single-digit CI runs, and the failure is a billing failure in the middle of a slice, not a build failure you can debug. Second, an LFS object is permanent: every engine upgrade adds another 174 MB to the repository's storage forever, and this repository expects to outlive the tool by design ("Every tool this system currently uses must be replaceable without invalidating a single line below", blueprint.md). Carrying the tool inside the artefact that is supposed to survive its replacement is the wrong shape. Third, it makes this repository a redistribution point for someone else's unversioned nightly build, whose licence we have not established. None of those is fatal alone. Together they are enough, and the thing they buy — "no network at build time" — is a property we do not actually have anyway, because CI already reaches PyPI on every run via `uv sync --frozen`.

**Fetching unpinned, argued properly.** Simplest possible machinery: one `git clone --branch binaries`, done. It has one genuine virtue nobody else has — you cannot rot, because you always have the newest fix for whatever DuckDB bug bites next, and this engine has DuckDB bugs (see below). Against that: a branch called `binaries` carrying nightly builds is a branch that will be force-pushed. The day it is, the DAB layer changes underneath a green history, and `git bisect` — which conventions.md §7 makes load-bearing ("Bisect is only worth anything if every point in history is a working system") — starts lying, because the same commit now builds a different warehouse. Unpinned fetch is not a different option from pinned fetch; it is pinned fetch with the pin deleted.

**Local path only, argued properly.** Honest about where the binary actually comes from — someone put it there — and it costs zero machinery. It is also the only option that works in a genuinely airgapped environment. But it does not answer the question that was asked, which is "CI has to work". CI has never seen the binary; something has to put it on the runner, and "a documented manual step" on a hosted ephemeral runner is not a step, it is a wish. What it *is* good for is the escape hatch, so I keep it: `DAANA_CLI` pointing at a path, still hash-verified against the same manifest. The verification is what turns it from a story into a contract.

**Container image, argued properly.** The strongest reproducibility of the five: a digest-pinned image pins the binary *and* the glibc it was linked against, and a 174 MB Go binary from an unknown build environment is exactly the kind of thing that fails on the wrong base image. `docker run` in CI is one line. Two things sink it. It pins nothing extra unless you pin the digest, which is the same hash-in-a-manifest discipline one layer further out with more moving parts; and it makes Docker a prerequisite for a project whose entire toolchain is otherwise `uv sync`, for the sake of running one statically-linked executable. daana-cli 0.7.0 removed its own Docker sidecar ("Everything now runs inside the Go binary itself. The local Postgres sidecar is gone - no external database, no Docker port, no second process") — reintroducing a container to run the binary that was made containerless is moving against the tool's own grain. Revisit if the binary turns out to have runtime library dependencies we cannot satisfy on a plain runner.

**Writing the focal generator ourselves, argued properly, because it deserves it.** This is not a strawman. Look at what we are proposing to depend on: a binary that self-reports as `nightly`; whose `--help` advertises "Multi-database support (PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, Oracle, SQL Server)" and does *not* list DuckDB; whose 0.7.0 release post names PostgreSQL and BigQuery as the only tested environments; which creates `<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` tables on DuckDB and never populates them while reporting the `execute_idfr_pipelines` phase as succeeding; which corrupts a base table by one row per run under a strategy the user selected, invisibly; and which reports "the framework is not installed" when the real problem is a file lock. Writing it ourselves would give us a generator we can test, a physical model we control, and no acquisition problem at all. What sinks it is the blueprint, not the effort: "Structure enforces the consistent application of business definitions; it does not produce the definitions... The effort saved on mechanism is meant to be redirected to meaning, not removed" (design-of-analytical-systems). Building the mechanism is precisely the effort the architecture wants redirected. And what we would be reimplementing is not trivial: spike 2 showed `view_CUSTOMER_hist` is a genuine gaps-and-islands window reconstruction that carries unchanged attributes forward across value-runs and aligns attributes sourced from *different tables under different ingestion strategies* onto the same `eff_tmstp`. That is the hard part of ensemble modelling and it works. We take the engine and we cage it.

**The cage is the real decision.** Every one of the engine's defects above is silent. None of them fails a build. That is what makes a numbered rule set the substance of this record rather than an appendix to it: daana accepts wrong mappings without complaint, so the honesty of the DAB layer is exactly equal to the rules we impose on the mapping files plus the tests that check them.

Rule M4 — `ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG` everywhere, `FULL` forbidden outright — is the one that had to be got right, and the two spikes settle it jointly rather than separately. Spike 1 established that `das__staged` is append-style *by construction*: "Two identical runs produce 240 rows for 120 distinct orders." Spike 2 established what `FULL` does to such a source: "customers mapping switched to `ingestion_strategy: FULL` while `das__staged.customers` held 2 rows for C001... run4: 23, run5: 24, run6: 25 (+1 every execute)... `view_CUSTOMER` stayed at 3 rows and `view_CUSTOMER_hist` at 4 rows throughout — the corruption never surfaces in the views." Unbounded growth, invisible to every consumer, and "switching back to FULL_LOG stops the growth but does NOT clean up the 5 rows already leaked." The obvious alternative — make `das__staged` a latest-per-key snapshot so that `FULL` becomes correct, which spike 2 finding 10 proves it is against a one-row-per-key view — must be rejected on principle, not on taste. It would make DAB's history a function of *how often the build ran* rather than of what DAS holds, and a cold rebuild would collapse every entity to a single version. Blueprint S2 exists for exactly this: "DAB and DAR must be rebuildable from DAS at any time without going back to the source." A snapshot staging view breaks S2 in the only way that matters. So the staged view keeps every version, and `FULL` is therefore unusable here, permanently, not situationally. `TRANSACTIONAL` (proven working in spike 2 finding 17) and `INCREMENTAL` are deferred rather than forbidden, because both introduce warehouse-resident watermark state and the abort path documented in `execute --help` ("If batch_history has prior 'F' or 'R' rows but no successful 'C' row... the framework aborts that pipeline"), which trades our reproducibility property for a speed we do not need at 830 orders.

The remaining rules follow from the same principle — that anything the engine will silently accept must be forbidden by us or asserted by a test. M6/M7 (expression purity) exist because a `transformation_expression` is inlined verbatim into generated SQL: a subquery there is a hand-written join, which contradicts "You don't write the joins - the model does" (why-we-built-daana), and an aggregate there is aggregation inside DAB, which contradicts B5. M3 (one `primary_keys` list per entity, identical across every table block) exists because spike 2 finding 14 showed `<entity>_key` is the natural key value verbatim — `'C001'`, `'O100'` — with `_idfr` empty, so there is no identifier-resolution layer to catch two table blocks that disagree about what identifies an instance; the mistake would just create two orders. M14 (the DAR allow-list) exists because three separate DuckDB-specific findings all point the same way: `_focal` and `_idfr` are created and never populated, so a DAR generator that joins to them returns nothing and reports zero rather than failing; `view_<entity>_with_rel` has a column list "byte-identical to `view_<entity>`", so its name is an active lie; and the presentation views wrap DuckDB table macros invisible to `information_schema`, so any name-construction or inventory code has to look in `duckdb_functions()` too. M16 turns that last one into a general rule: *names are looked up, never constructed*.

**On UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, which is the question I expected to answer the other way.** The case against keeping it is real and I will state it at full strength. daana-cli 0.7.0 explicitly relaxed the requirement — "Entity IDs, workflow IDs, attribute names, and relationship names now accept any casing... The checker and compiler previously enforced UPPER_SNAKE_CASE" — and removed the three lint rules that enforced it, so the tool no longer supports the convention at all. Spike 2 then showed the consequence on our platform: DuckDB preserves the casing, giving `view_CUSTOMER`, `CUSTOMER_desc`, `ORDER_CUSTOMER_x`, where PostgreSQL folds the same model to lowercase. So the same `model.yaml` produces differently-named objects on two platforms — in a system whose stated design is "platform behind one seam". Lowercasing the model ids would erase that difference, erase the two-casing world, let `RF06` back into sqlfluff (it is currently excluded, and it is a correctness rule, not a style rule), and mean no identifier anywhere ever needs a quote. That is a genuinely strong case and it nearly wins.

It loses on two counts. The first is that the portability benefit is already bought elsewhere: rule M16 requires every DAB object name to be *read from the catalog and compared case-insensitively*, a rule I need anyway because of the table macros and the empty `_focal` tables. Once no name is constructed, the platform difference is unobservable, and spike 2 confirmed the consumer side is safe regardless — `dab.view_customer`, `dab.VIEW_CUSTOMER`, `dab."view_CUSTOMER"` and `dab."view_customer"` all resolve to the same object. The second is the argument conventions.md itself makes: the visual break is what makes a leak obvious on sight. There is exactly one file in this system where business vocabulary and source vocabulary appear on the same line — the mapping. `{id: SHIP_COUNTRY, transformation_expression: ship_country}` is legible at a glance in a way `{id: ship_country, transformation_expression: ship_country}` is not, and mapping edits are the highest-frequency change in the DAB layer. §1.2's hard rule against source names in DAB has no mechanical enforcement now that daana's lint rules are gone; the casing break is the cheapest thing that makes a violation visible to a reviewer. Decisive corroboration that the convention was written knowing this: `.sqlfluff` already excludes RF06 with the comment "RF06 fires on every mixed-case identifier crossing over from DAB", and §3 already says "Identifiers crossing over from DAB are double-quoted". The cost of mixed-case DAB identifiers was priced into this repository before the spike ran. The convention survives contact. It is not free, and I record the price in the consequences.

**Single-writer discipline.** Spike 2 finding 11 is the most operationally dangerous thing either spike found, because it is a correct-looking wrong answer: with any other connection open — "read-write OR READ-ONLY" — `execute` fails with "daana framework is not installed on the remote database. Run 'daana-cli install' first", and "no 'lock', 'conflict' or 'duckdb' string appears anywhere in the debug output". An operator who believes that message runs `install`, which will fail the same way, and the obvious next move is to start deleting schemas. The design response is two-part and both parts are machinery, so both are test-first. First, prevention: one build process holds an exclusive `flock` on `warehouse.duckdb.lock` for its whole run, and the platform seam grows an explicit *detached* state — every Python DuckDB connection is closed and asserted closed before the engine subprocess is spawned, and reopened afterwards. daana-cli is the only writer during its own phase because it is structurally the only holder. Second, translation: the subprocess wrapper matches the known stderr string and replaces it with a message naming the file, the real cause, the fact that other *readers* count, and the explicit instruction that `install` is not the fix. That translation is generic machinery with no data vocabulary in it (conventions §5), which means it can be unit-tested against the recorded stderr — and must be, because the string comes from a nightly binary and will eventually be reworded, at which point the test fails and tells us, rather than the translation silently going quiet.
result.concreteShape:
**Files this decision creates (paths relative to the repo root).**

```
dab/model.yaml                    the only place the data is explained
dab/mappings/order-mapping.yaml   one file per entity
dab/workflow.yaml                 produced by `daana-cli generate workflow`, then edited
dab/connections.yaml              one profile, `dev`
dab/config.yaml                   whatever `generate`/`init` emits; always passed with --config
dab/engine.lock                   the engine pin (see below)
src/adss/platform.py              the one platform seam: Warehouse, exclusive(), detached()
src/adss/engine.py                resolve/verify the binary; invoke it; translate its errors
tests/test_engine_pin.py          hash + self-report must match dab/engine.lock
tests/test_mapping_rules.py       M1/M3/M4/M5 checked against dab/mappings/*.yaml
tests/test_dab_build.py           cold rebuild, determinism, history completeness
.gitignore                        add `*.duckdb.lock` and `dab/logs/`
```

---

**`dab/model.yaml`** — slice 1 has one entity and no `relationships:` block, because there is nothing yet for ORDER to relate to.

```yaml
entities:
  - id: "ORDER"
    name: "ORDER"
    definition: "A request from a customer for goods, accepted by the business as a commitment to supply them."
    description: "One order is one such commitment. It exists from the moment it is accepted."
    attributes:
      - id: "ORDER_ID"
        name: "ORDER_ID"
        definition: "The identifier the business uses when it refers to one order."
        type: "STRING"
        effective_timestamp: false
      - id: "PLACED_ON"
        name: "PLACED_ON"
        definition: "The moment the business accepted the order and it began to exist."
        type: "START_TIMESTAMP"
      - id: "SHIP_COUNTRY"
        name: "SHIP_COUNTRY"
        definition: "The country the business has undertaken to deliver the order to."
        type: "STRING"
        effective_timestamp: true
```

`type` values are constrained to `STRING`, `NUMBER`, `UNIT`, `START_TIMESTAMP`, `END_TIMESTAMP`. There is no plain timestamp type, so `PLACED_ON` takes `START_TIMESTAMP` — the entity's own beginning-of-life business instant, which is semantically what an order date is — and omits `effective_timestamp`, matching every START/END-typed attribute in the DMDL example. `ORDER_ID` carries `effective_timestamp: false` because it is the key.

---

**`dab/mappings/order-mapping.yaml`**

```yaml
entity_id: ORDER
mapping_groups:
  - name: default_mapping_group
    tables:
      - connection: dev
        table: das__staged.orders
        primary_keys: [order_id]
        ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG
        entity_effective_timestamp_expression: extracted_at
        attributes:
          - {id: ORDER_ID, transformation_expression: cast(order_id AS VARCHAR)}
          - {id: PLACED_ON, transformation_expression: order_date}
          - {id: SHIP_COUNTRY, transformation_expression: ship_country}
```

Flow mappings for the attribute rows are explicitly blessed by conventions §4 ("a mapping attribute") and unpadded, so a longer expression is a one-line diff. `.yamllint.yaml` sets `braces.max-spaces-inside: 1` and `line-length.max: 160`, so this passes the gate as written. The single `cast(...)` is the only kind permitted by M7 — the one needed to reach the declared DMDL type, spelled `cast(x AS T)` per conventions §3, never `::`.

---

**`dab/connections.yaml`** — the exact shape spike 2 proved works, with `database` made relative to this file's own directory.

```yaml
connections:
  dev:
    type: duckdb
    database: ../warehouse.duckdb
    target_schema: dab
    stage_schema: dab__stage
    metadata_schema: dab__meta
```

`../warehouse.duckdb` resolves to the same file whether the engine resolves it against the process cwd or against `connections.yaml` — because M12 fixes cwd to `dab/`, which is where `connections.yaml` lives. Spike 2's open question ("whether the relative path is resolved against the CWD or against the connections.yaml location") is thereby made unable to matter.

---

**`dab/workflow.yaml`** — shape below; **key names are taken from `daana-cli generate workflow --model ./model.yaml -o ./workflow.yaml` and then edited**, never invented. `check workflow` prints both a name and a numeric Workflow ID (spike 2: `Workflow: BOOK_RETAILER_WORKFLOW / Workflow ID: 1424339281`); the number is engine-derived and must never appear in any file or script we write.

```yaml
workflow:
  id: "ADSS"
  name: "ADSS"
  model: "./model.yaml"
  connection: "dev"
  mappings:
    - "./mappings/order-mapping.yaml"
```

---

**`dab/engine.lock`** — the pin. Content-addressed, because there is no version.

```yaml
engine: daana-cli
source:
  repo: "https://github.com/mattiasthalen/ADSS-fable-POC"
  ref: "binaries"
  path: "bin/linux-amd64/daana-cli"
platform: "linux-amd64"
sha256: "492ddf86ab3361104f503a6e0cc9ce412ec6dfbcc744e7c30ae23eb0ccc739d3"
self_report: "daana-cli version nightly, commit 113d5a6a77c123679656a9c769c6b88123341f36, built at 2026-09-04T22:13:46Z"
```

Resolution order in `src/adss/engine.py`: `$DAANA_CLI` → `~/.cache/adss/daana-cli/<sha256>/daana-cli` → fetch (`git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout --depth 1 --branch binaries`, then `git lfs pull --include <path>`) into the cache. Whichever path wins, both checks run before any invocation: `sha256` of the file equals `engine.lock`, and the binary's own `-v` output equals `self_report` verbatim. CI adds `actions/cache` keyed on the sha256, so the 174 MB fetch happens once per pin, not once per run.

---

**Invocation (M12), from `src/adss/engine.py`, cwd = `dab/`:**

```
daana-cli check model     --config ./config.yaml --no-tui --format json
daana-cli check mapping   --config ./config.yaml --no-tui --format json --skip-schema-validation   # gate: offline, no DB
daana-cli check mapping   --config ./config.yaml --no-tui --format json --connections ./connections.yaml --connection dev --strict
daana-cli check workflow  --config ./config.yaml --no-tui --format json
daana-cli install         --config ./config.yaml --no-tui --connections ./connections.yaml --connection dev
daana-cli deploy          --config ./config.yaml --no-tui --connections ./connections.yaml --connection dev --strict
daana-cli execute         --config ./config.yaml --no-tui --connections ./connections.yaml --connection dev
```

`--config` is never omitted: `daana-cli --help` documents a fallback to `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/daana/config.yaml`, and `init` creates one there, so an invocation without `--config` is a build whose behaviour depends on the developer's home directory. Recovery from the FULL-class leak, should a mapping ever regress, is `execute --full-refresh --entity ORDER --yes`, which `execute --help` documents as deleting one entity's tables and its `batch_history` rows while preserving views, functions and metadata structure — no `install`/`deploy` re-run.

---

**Physical shapes DAR reads (column names from spike 2's `DESCRIBE`).**

`dab.view_ORDER` → `ORDER_key VARCHAR`, `order_id VARCHAR`, `placed_on TIMESTAMP`, `ship_country VARCHAR`. The key column keeps the entity-id casing with a lowercase `_key` suffix; attribute columns are the lower-cased attribute ids. So the slice-1 DAR read, with DAB identifiers double-quoted per conventions §3:

```sql
SELECT
    o."ORDER_key" AS order_key,
    o.order_id AS order_id,
    o.placed_on AS placed_on,
    o.ship_country AS ship_country
FROM dab.view_order AS o
```

Allow-list (M14): `dab.view_<ENTITY>`, `dab.view_<ENTITY>_hist`, `dab.view_<SOURCE>_<NAME>_<TARGET>`. Denied by name: `<ENTITY>_focal`, `<ENTITY>_idfr`, `<ENTITY>_desc`, `<SRC>_<TGT>_x`, `v_*`, `f_*`, `view_<ENTITY>_with_rel`, and the whole of `dab__stage` and `dab__meta`.

**Inventory / health check (build-only carve-out), both queries required** because the views wrap table macros:

```sql
SELECT table_schema, table_name, table_type FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema IN ('dab', 'dab__stage', 'dab__meta');

SELECT schema_name, function_name, function_type FROM duckdb_functions()
WHERE schema_name IN ('dab', 'dab__stage', 'dab__meta');
```

---

**The numbered rule set** (each entry: rule — why — severity). It belongs in conventions.md §1.2 as a DAB subsection.

| # | Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | A mapping table's `table:` is exactly `das__staged.<contract stem>`. Never `das__raw`, never a path or `read_parquet()`, never a `dab` object. | Blueprint F3. `das__raw` is an untyped payload column; unpacking it from a mapping would move S3's strict boundary into the wrong layer. | Hard |
| M2 | One mapping file per entity at `dab/mappings/<entity>-mapping.yaml`, first produced by `daana-cli generate mapping --entity <ID>`; after any model change, reconciled with `daana-cli merge mapping --diff` before the diff is committed. | The key set is the engine's, not ours. `merge --diff` makes a model change's effect on mappings reviewable instead of remembered. | Hard |
| M3 | The instance key is declared once, as `primary_keys:` naming the das__staged column(s) carrying the source's own key, identical in every table block of that entity. No attribute re-derives or re-encodes it. | `<entity>_key` is that value verbatim and `_idfr` is empty on DuckDB, so two blocks disagreeing silently create two instances of one thing. | Hard |
| M4 | `ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG` on every table. `FULL` is forbidden. `INCREMENTAL`/`TRANSACTIONAL` require an ADR. | `das__staged` is append-style by construction; `FULL` against it leaks one `_desc` row per execute, unbounded, invisible in every view. | Hard |
| M5 | `entity_effective_timestamp_expression:` is the bare column `extracted_at`. No expression, no `COALESCE`, no source business date. | Already decided; a business date makes `eff_tmstp` non-monotonic and makes "what did we know when" unanswerable. | Hard |
| M6 | A `transformation_expression` is a pure, single-row function of columns of its own table: no subquery, join, aggregate, window, cross-schema reference, or non-deterministic function. | It is inlined into generated SQL unchecked. A subquery is a hand-written join; an aggregate is aggregation inside DAB (B5). | Hard |
| M7 | It may name one column, optionally wrapped in the single `cast(x AS T)` needed to reach the declared DMDL type. Anything more — `CASE`, `COALESCE` to a sentinel, concatenating two columns — only if the attribute's `definition` states that rule. | B8: a rule living only in the mapping is a second, invisible definition of the data. | Hard |
| M8 | Do not cast numerics for width or scale. | Everything is materialised `DECIMAL(28,8)` regardless; the cast misleads the reader. Formatting is DAR's job. | Guideline |
| M9 | Relationship `id` == `name` == the bare verb phrase (`IS_PLACED_BY`), UPPER_SNAKE_CASE; `source_entity_id` is the many side. Never write the composed sentence into the id. | The engine composes `view_<SOURCE>_<NAME>_<TARGET>`; putting the sentence in the id doubles the entity names in the emitted object. | Hard |
| M10 | A relationship is declared on the mapping table of its **source** (many) entity — the one table holding both keys on one row. | The other direction needs a join, which M6 forbids. | Hard |
| M11 | At most one relationship per ordered entity pair. A second needs an ADR and a test proving both survive. | The cross table is `<SOURCE>_<TARGET>_x` with no relationship name in it — a second edge may collide. | Hard |
| M12 | Every invocation comes from the build, cwd `dab/`, with `--no-tui` and explicit `--config`, `--connections`, `--connection`. | `--help` documents an ambient `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` fallback; and co-locating cwd with `connections.yaml` neutralises the unresolved relative-path question. | Hard |
| M13 | The engine runs only inside the build's exclusive lock, with every Python connection closed first; its "framework is not installed" stderr is re-reported as a busy-file error. | Any other connection, read-only included, produces that message. | Hard |
| M14 | DAR reads only `view_<ENTITY>`, `view_<ENTITY>_hist`, `view_<SOURCE>_<NAME>_<TARGET>`. | `_focal`/`_idfr` are empty; `_desc`/`_x` are keyed on `type_key` re-derived at deploy; `_with_rel` carries no relationship keys despite its name. | Hard |
| M15 | A count-of-instances measure reads `view_<ENTITY>`, never `view_<ENTITY>_hist`. | `_hist` is compacted to one row per value-run, so `COUNT(*)` over it counts value-states, not instances. | Hard |
| M16 | DAB object names are read from the catalog (both `information_schema.tables` and `duckdb_functions()`) and compared case-insensitively. Never constructed. | DuckDB preserves the model's casing, PostgreSQL folds it; a constructed name is a platform assumption sitting behind a platform seam. | Hard |
| M17 | Entity, attribute and relationship ids stay UPPER_SNAKE_CASE with `id` == `name`. | conventions §1.2, unchanged; the visual break is what makes a source-name leak visible in the one file where both vocabularies meet. | Hard |
| M18 | The engine is resolved through `dab/engine.lock` and verified by sha256 *and* self-report on every build. Changing it is its own commit whose diff is that file. | It self-reports as `nightly`; content is its only identity. | Hard |
